title: Defence of Seneca and Plutarch
paragraphs: The familiarity I have with these two authors, and the help they have given to my age and to my book — which is, after all, wholly compiled out of what I have borrowed from them — obliges me to stand up for their honour.

As to Seneca: among the millions of little pamphlets that people of the so-called reformed religion scatter abroad in defence of their cause (some of them coming from so good a hand that it is a pity his pen is not employed on a better subject), I once saw one which, trying to construct a parallel between the government of our late poor King Charles IX and that of Nero, compared the late Cardinal of Lorraine with Seneca. Their fortunes were said to be alike in that both had been prime ministers to their princes, and their manners, characters, and conduct were said to be very nearly the same. In my opinion, this does the Cardinal a very great honour. I am one of those who have a high esteem for his wit, his eloquence, his zeal for religion and the service of his king, and his good fortune in having lived in an age when it was so unusual, so rare, and so necessary for the public good to have a churchman of high birth and dignity who was equal to his office. But to be honest, I do not think his ability comes within many degrees of Seneca's, nor was his virtue as clean, complete, or steady.

Now the book I am speaking of, to advance its case, gives a very damaging description of Seneca, borrowing its approach from Dion the historian — whose testimony I do not trust at all. Dion is inconsistent: after calling Seneca at one moment very wise and a mortal enemy to Nero's vices, he elsewhere makes him out to be greedy, a usurer, ambitious, soft, sensual, and a fraud as a philosopher. Yet Seneca's virtue shows up so lively and vigorously in his own writings, and he answers the charges so clearly — the riches, the lavish way of life — that I cannot believe any testimony against it. And besides, in matters of this sort it is much more reasonable to trust Roman historians than Greeks and foreigners. Tacitus and the rest speak honourably of both his life and his death, and present him as a thoroughly excellent and virtuous man. I will allege only one further reproach against Dion's report, and I cannot pass it over: his judgment of Roman affairs is so weak that he dares to defend Julius Caesar's cause against Pompey, and Antony's against Cicero.

Now to Plutarch. Jean Bodin is a good author of our times, with much sounder judgment than the crowd of scribblers of his age, and deserves to be read and considered. I find him, though, a little bold in a passage of his Method of History, where he accuses Plutarch not only of ignorance (which I would have let pass — that is beyond my judgment) but of "often writing things incredible and absolutely fabulous." Those are his own words. If he had merely said Plutarch reports things otherwise than they really were, that would be no great reproach: what we have not seen we have to take from other hands and on trust. I myself notice that Plutarch sometimes deliberately tells the same story two different ways — Hannibal's judgment of the three greatest captains there ever were, for example, goes one way in the Life of Flamininus and another in the Life of Pyrrhus. But to charge him with having taken impossible and incredible things as ready money is to accuse the most judicious author in the world of lacking judgment. And here is Bodin's example: "as when," he says, "Plutarch relates that a Spartan boy let his guts be torn out by a fox-cub he had stolen and hidden under his cloak, rather than let his theft be discovered." To begin with, I find the example badly chosen, because it is very hard to put a limit on what the soul's faculties can endure, whereas we have better grounds for knowing the limits of the body's strength. If I had been him, I would have picked an example of the second kind, and there are some less credible — among others Plutarch's tale of Pyrrhus, who, wounded as he was, struck one of his enemies, fully armed from head to foot, such a blow with his sword that he split him from crown to seat, so that the body fell apart in two pieces. In that example I find no great miracle, and I do not accept the excuse Plutarch makes by adding "as it is said," to suspend our belief. Unless it is in things received on authority, out of reverence for antiquity or religion, he would never have admitted, or asked us to believe, things incredible in themselves; and that the words "as it is said" are not really doing that work here is easy to see, because elsewhere on the same theme — the patience of Spartan children — he gives examples from his own time more unlikely than the fox-cub story. Cicero before him gave the same testimony, having (as he says) been on the spot: that even in their day there were children who, in the trial of patience they underwent at the altar of Diana, let themselves be whipped till the blood streamed down their bodies — not only without crying out, but without so much as a groan, and some until they voluntarily lost their lives. Plutarch, among a hundred other witnesses, also reports that at a sacrifice a live coal fell into the sleeve of a Spartan boy who was burning incense; he let his whole arm be roasted until the smell of his flesh reached those around him. By their custom there was nothing for which their reputation was more at stake, and for which they would suffer more blame and disgrace, than being caught in theft. I am so fully convinced of the greatness of those people that this story does not seem to me, as it does to Bodin, incredible — I do not even find it rare or strange. Spartan history is full of a thousand crueller and rarer examples; on this subject it is one long miracle.

Marcellinus, on the subject of theft, reports that in his day no kind of torture could compel the Egyptians, when caught in the act (and they were a people much given to it), so much as to give their names.

A Spanish peasant, racked for the names of the accomplices in the murder of the praetor Lucius Piso, shouted out at the height of the torment that his friends should not desert him but watch in full confidence — that no pain had the power to force one word of confession from him. That was all they got out of him the first day. The next day, as they were leading him to a second session on the rack, he wrenched himself out of his guards' hands and ran his head violently against a wall, beating his own brains out.

Epicharis, having tired out and glutted the cruelty of Nero's torturers — having endured their fire, their beating, their racks for a whole day without one syllable of confession about the conspiracy — was brought back to the rack the next day with her limbs almost torn to pieces. She slipped the ribbon of her robe through a running noose over one of the arms of her chair, suddenly thrust her head into it, and with the weight of her own body hanged herself. Having the courage to die in that manner — is it not fair to assume that she had deliberately given up her life to the trial of her resolve the day before, to mock the tyrant and encourage others to a similar attempt?

And anyone who will ask our troopers what they have seen in our civil wars will find examples of patience and stubborn resolution in this miserable age of ours, and among a rabble even softer than the Egyptians, that are worthy to be compared with what we have just related of Spartan virtue.

I know there have been simple peasants among us who have let the soles of their feet be grilled on a gridiron, their fingertips crushed with the cock of a pistol, and their bleeding eyes squeezed out of their heads by a cord twisted around their brows, before they would so much as agree to a ransom. I once saw a man left stark naked for dead in a ditch, his neck black and swollen, with the rope still around it that they had used to drag him all night at a horse's tail, his body wounded in a hundred places by daggers — not stabbed to kill him, but to torment and terrify him. He had endured it all, even to being beyond speech and feeling, resolved (as he told me himself) to die a thousand deaths rather than promise anything — and he had effectively borne one already in pain. He was, on top of that, one of the richest farmers in the country. How many have been seen patiently letting themselves be burnt and roasted for opinions taken on trust from others, and which they themselves did not understand? I have known a hundred women — and Gascony has a certain prerogative for obstinacy — whom you could sooner have made eat fire than give up an opinion they had taken hold of in anger. They only grow more exasperated under blows and constraint. And whoever invented the story of the woman who, in spite of every correction, threat, and beating, kept calling her husband a lousy knave, and who, when ducked over her head in water, lifted her hands above her head and made the sign of cracking lice — that storyteller was inventing a tale whose living image we see every day in the obstinacy of women. And obstinacy is the sister of constancy, at least in toughness and staying power.

We are not to judge what is possible and what is not by what is credible or incredible to our own understanding. As I have said elsewhere, it is a great fault — and yet one most men are guilty of, and I do not raise it now to point at Bodin — to refuse to believe of someone else what we ourselves could not or would not do. Everyone thinks the sovereign stamp of human nature is impressed in himself, and that all others must take their measure from it, so that any conduct that is not like his own must be faked or false. Is some action or capacity of another's put before such a man? The first thing he calls into consultation is his own example: as matters go with him, they must go with the rest of the world. A dangerous and intolerable folly. For my part, I consider some men, especially among the ancients, infinitely beyond me; and though I see clearly that I cannot come within a thousand paces of them, I still keep them in sight and judge what raises them so high, because I sense some seeds of it in myself — just as I do of the extreme meanness of certain other minds, which neither astonishes me nor strains my belief. I see clearly enough the moves those great souls make to lift themselves to such a pitch, and I admire their grandeur; I would gladly imitate the flights I think the bravest, and although I lack the wings, my judgment can at least follow along. The other example Bodin holds up as "incredible and wholly fabulous" in Plutarch is that "Agesilaus was fined by the Ephori for having engrossed the hearts and affections of his citizens to himself alone." Here I see no sign of falsity at all. Plutarch is speaking of things that must have been better known to him than to us; and it was no new thing in Greece for men to be punished and exiled for being too popular — witness the ostracism and petalism.

There is in this same passage another charge against Plutarch I cannot stomach, where Bodin says that Plutarch sincerely paralleled Romans with Romans and Greeks with Greeks, but not Romans with Greeks: witness, he says, Demosthenes and Cicero, Cato and Aristides, Sulla and Lysander, Marcellus and Pelopidas, Pompey and Agesilaus — and that he favoured the Greeks by giving them such unequal partners. This is really to attack what is best in Plutarch and most worth praising; for in his Parallels (which is the most admirable part of all his work, and the one with which, I think, he was himself most pleased) the fidelity and sincerity of his judgments equal their depth and weight. He is a philosopher who teaches us virtue. Let us see whether we can defend him from this charge of falsity and bias. All I can imagine giving rise to the censure is the great and shining glamour of the Roman names we have in our minds: it does not seem likely to us that Demosthenes could rival the glory of a consul, proconsul, and praetor of that great Republic. But if you consider the truth of the thing, and the men in themselves — which is Plutarch's chief aim — and weigh their characters, their natures, and their parts rather than their fortunes, I think (contrary to Bodin) that Cicero and the elder Cato fall far short of the men they are compared with. For Bodin's purpose I would sooner have picked the younger Cato paired with Phocion: in that couple there would have been a more plausible inequality, in the Roman's favour. As for Marcellus, Sulla, and Pompey, I see well enough that their war-exploits are greater and more full of pomp and glory than those of the Greeks Plutarch matches them with; but the bravest and most virtuous actions, in war as elsewhere, are not always the most renowned. I often see the names of captains darkened by the brilliance of others of less merit — witness Labienus, Ventidius, Telesinus, and a few more. And to take it that way: if I had to complain on the Greek side, could I not say that Camillus was much less comparable to Themistocles, the Gracchi to Agis and Cleomenes, and Numa to Lycurgus? But it is folly to judge in one glance things that have so many faces. When Plutarch compares them, he does not for all that make them equal — and who could more learnedly and honestly have marked their distinctions? Does he set the victories, the feats of arms, the strength of the armies Pompey commanded, and his triumphs against those of Agesilaus? "I do not believe," he says, "that Xenophon himself, were he alive, with full leave to write whatever he pleased in Agesilaus' favour, would dare put them in the comparison." Does he speak of paralleling Lysander to Sulla? "There is," he says, "no comparison, either in the number of victories or in the risks of battles, for Lysander only won two naval battles." This is not to belittle the Romans: simply by naming them alongside the Greeks he can have done them no harm, whatever the gap between them — and Plutarch does not set them flatly opposite each other. There is no overall verdict; he only compares the pieces and circumstances one by one and gives each a separate judgment. So if anyone wants to convict him of partiality he ought to point to one of those particular judgments, or to say in general that he was wrong to match a given Greek with a given Roman when there were others better suited to pair him with.

title: The story of Spurina
paragraphs: Philosophy thinks she has not wasted her talent when she gives reason sovereignty over the soul and authority to restrain our appetites. Among those appetites, those who think none more violent than the ones springing from love also hold that they seize body and soul together, possessing the whole man — so that health itself depends on them, and medicine is sometimes forced to play pimp on their behalf. But you could argue, on the other side, that being mixed with the body actually weakens them: such desires are subject to satiety, and can be answered by material remedies.

Many, set on ridding their souls of this appetite's constant alarms, have used cutting and amputation on the rebellious parts. Others have subdued its force and ardour by frequent applications of cold things — snow, vinegar. Our ancestors' hair shirts had the same purpose: a cloth woven of horsehair, of which some made shirts and others belts, to torture and discipline their loins. A prince told me, not long ago, that in his youth, on a great festival day at the court of King Francis I, where everyone was dressed splendidly, he insisted on putting on his father's hair shirt, which was still kept in the house. But however great his devotion, he could not stand to wear it until nightfall, and he was sick a long time after; he added that he did not believe there could be any youthful heat so fierce this remedy would not mortify — though perhaps he had never tried the most violent. For experience shows us that such heats often flare under rough and grubby clothes, and that a hair shirt does not always make those who wear it chaste.

Xenocrates went at the matter more harshly. His disciples, to test his continence, slipped Lais — that beautiful and famous courtesan — naked into his bed, armed only with her beauty, her wanton charms, and her love-philtres. Finding that, in spite of his reason and his philosophical rules, his unruly flesh was starting to mutiny, he had those members of his that had consented to the rebellion burned. By contrast, the passions that live entirely in the soul — ambition, greed, and the rest — give reason much more trouble, because she has to deal with them by her own means alone; nor are those appetites capable of satiety. They sharpen and grow with indulgence.

Julius Caesar's example alone is enough to show the difference between these appetites. No man was ever more given to amorous pleasures than he was: one proof is the peculiar care he took of his body, going so far as to use the most lascivious means then in fashion — having all the hairs of his body plucked off, and rubbing himself all over with perfumes with the most painstaking attention. And he was a handsome man in himself: fair-skinned, tall, lively, full-faced, with quick hazel eyes — at least if we can trust Suetonius; the statues of him in Rome do not fully answer that description on every point. Apart from his wives, of whom he changed four — and leaving aside the affair of his youth with Nicomedes, king of Bithynia — he had the maidenhead of the famous Cleopatra, queen of Egypt, as the little Caesarion she bore him bears witness. He also courted Eunoe, queen of Mauretania, and in Rome Postumia, the wife of Servius Sulpicius; Lollia, the wife of Gabinius; Tertulla, the wife of Crassus; and even Mucia, wife of the great Pompey — which, the Roman historians say, was the reason Pompey divorced her, though Plutarch confesses he could not tell for certain. The two Curios, father and son, later reproached Pompey, when he married Caesar's daughter, with having made himself son-in-law to a man who had cuckolded him, and whom he used to call Aegisthus. Besides all these, he kept Servilia, Cato's sister and the mother of Marcus Brutus — from which, most people believe, came his great affection for Brutus, who had been born at a time when it was likely he was his son. So I think I have reason to take him for a man extremely given to debauchery, and of a very amorous constitution. But his other passion, ambition — by which he was infinitely struck — rose up to challenge the first, and that one was promptly forced to give way.

And here, calling to mind Mehmed, who won Constantinople and finally wiped out the Greek name, I do not know where these two appetites were so evenly balanced as in him: equally an indefatigable lecher and an indefatigable soldier. But where they met and jostled in his life, the warlike passion always got the better of the amorous one, and the latter, even out of its natural season, never regained full sovereignty over the other until he had reached extreme old age and could no longer bear the rigours of war.

What is reported of Ladislaus, king of Naples, as a counter-example is very striking. A great captain, brave and ambitious, he set up as the chief end of his ambition the pursuit of his pleasure and the enjoyment of some rare and excellent beauty. His death sealed the rest. By a long and grinding siege he had reduced Florence to such distress that the citizens were forced to negotiate surrender. He agreed to let them be, provided they handed over to him a beautiful girl he had heard of in their city. They had to give in — averting public ruin by a private wrong. She was the daughter of a famous physician of his day. Finding himself caught in so foul a necessity, he resolved on a desperate stroke. While everyone was helping to deck out his daughter, adorning her with ornaments and jewels to make her more agreeable to her new lover, he gave her a richly embroidered handkerchief, exquisitely perfumed — an item ladies there never go without — to use at the first encounter. This handkerchief, poisoned with all his skill, was rubbed between their warm flesh and open pores, and so suddenly let the poison in that their warm sweat at once turned cold and they died in each other's arms.

But back to Caesar. His pleasures never stole a single minute from him, nor a single step away from any occasion that might serve his advancement. This passion held such sovereignty over the rest, and possessed his soul with such absolute authority, that it steered him as it pleased. In truth, it troubles me, when I consider the greatness of this man and the wonderful gifts he had: learned to such a degree in every kind of knowledge that there is hardly a science he did not write on; so great an orator that many have preferred his eloquence to Cicero's — and he, I think, did not believe himself Cicero's inferior in that, since he wrote his two anti-Catos to counterbalance the eloquence Cicero had spent on his own Cato. And was there ever a soul so vigilant, so active, so patient under labour as his? No doubt it was adorned with many rare seeds of virtue, lively, natural, and not put on. He was strikingly sober. So far from being delicate in his diet that Oppius relates how one day at table, when medicated oil had been set before him instead of ordinary oil in some sauce, he ate heartily of it rather than embarrass his host. Another time he had his baker whipped for serving him bread finer than the rest of the company's. Cato himself used to say of him that he was the first sober man who ever set out to ruin his country. As for Cato calling him a drunkard one day, it happened like this: both were in the Senate when Catiline's conspiracy was being debated, with Caesar himself under suspicion, and someone came in and handed him a sealed letter. Cato, taking it for some communication from the conspirators, demanded it be put into his hands; Caesar was forced to comply, to avoid further suspicion. It turned out to be a love-letter Servilia, Cato's sister, had written him. Cato, having read it, threw it back at him, saying, "There, drunkard." That was rather a word of disdain and anger than a real reproach for the vice — as we often abuse those who annoy us with the first insulting word that comes to mouth, however inapt to the person we are angry with. To which one may add that the vice Cato charged him with is wonderfully near the one he had just caught Caesar in; for Bacchus and Venus, as the proverb says, are very willing partners. But to my taste, Venus is far livelier company when she is paired with sobriety. Examples of his sweetness and clemency to those who had offended him are countless — leaving aside those from the civil wars, which (as his own writings show plainly enough) he practised partly to flatter his enemies and make them less afraid of his coming dominion and victory. But I must also say that even if these examples are not proof of natural sweetness, they at least demonstrate an astonishing self-confidence and largeness of spirit in him. He often released whole armies of his enemies, after defeating them, without ransom, not even deigning to bind them by oath either to favour him or simply to take up arms against him no more. Three or four times he took some of Pompey's officers prisoner, and as often set them at liberty. Pompey declared all those his enemies who did not follow him to war; Caesar declared all those his friends who sat still and did not actually take up arms against him. To the officers of his who deserted to the other side, he sent on, moreover, their arms, horses, and equipage. The cities he had taken by force he left at full liberty to follow whichever side they pleased, imposing no garrison on them but the memory of his gentleness and clemency. On the day of his great battle at Pharsalia he gave strict and explicit orders that, unless absolutely forced, no one should lay a hand on the citizens of Rome. These were, in my view, very risky ways of proceeding, and it is no wonder that those in our own civil wars who fight, as he did, against the ancient state of their country do not follow his example. They are extraordinary means, suited only to Caesar's fortune and to his astonishing foresight in handling affairs. When I think of the incomparable greatness of his soul, I forgive victory for not being able to disentangle itself from him, even in so unjust and wicked a cause.

To return to his clemency. We have many striking examples from the time of his rule, when everything was in his hands. Caius Memmius had written some very sharp speeches against him, which he had answered just as sharply; yet he soon afterwards used his interest to make Memmius consul. Caius Calvus, who had composed several stinging epigrams against him, employed many of his friends to mediate a reconciliation; Caesar voluntarily resolved to write to him first. And our good Catullus, who had so roughly handled him under the name of Mamurra, came to apologise, and Caesar had him sit at his table that very same day. Having received word of some who were speaking ill of him, he did no more than declare in a public oration that he had been informed. He feared his enemies still less than he hated them. When certain conspiracies and plots against his life were uncovered to him, he was content to publish by proclamation that they were known to him, without prosecuting the conspirators further.

As to the regard he had for his friends: Caius Oppius, travelling with him, fell ill, and Caesar gave up the only lodging he had for himself and lay on the bare ground all night in the open air. As for his sense of justice, he had a beloved servant of his put to death for sleeping with a noble Roman's wife, although no complaint had been made. Never had any man more moderation in victory, or more steadiness in adverse fortune.

But all these good qualities were stifled and ruined by his furious ambition, which carried him away and led him astray so completely that one can easily argue this passion was the rudder of all his actions. From a generous man it made him a public thief, to fund that generosity and lavishness; and it drew from him that vile and unjust saying, that "if the most wicked and disreputable men in the world had been faithful in helping his advancement, he would cherish and promote them as much as he would the best of men." It intoxicated him with such extravagant vanity as to dare to boast, in the presence of his fellow citizens, that he had reduced the great commonwealth of Rome to a name without form or body; to say that his answers should henceforth stand as laws; to receive the senate, when it came to him, sitting; to suffer himself to be worshipped, and to have divine honours paid him in his own presence. To sum up: this one vice, in my view, ruined the richest and finest nature there ever was, and has made his name detestable to every good man, in that he built his glory on the ruin of his country and the overthrow of the greatest and most flourishing republic the world will ever see.

There are, on the other hand, many examples of great men whom pleasures have led to neglect the conduct of their affairs — Mark Antony and others. But wherever love and ambition stand in equal balance and come to grapple with equal force, I have no doubt the latter would carry off the prize.

To return to my subject. It is something to bridle our appetites by reason's argument, or to keep our members within their duty by violence. But to scourge ourselves on our neighbour's behalf — not only to divest ourselves of the charming passion that tickles us, of the pleasure of being agreeable to others and courted and loved by everyone, but to conceive a hatred for the very graces that produce that effect, and to condemn our beauty because it inflames others — of this, I admit, I have met few examples. But here is one. Spurina, a young man of Tuscany:
"Qualis gemma micat, fulvum quae dividit aurum, Aut collo decus, aut capiti: vel quale per artem Inclusum buxo aut Oricia terebintho Lucet ebur,"
["As a gem shines set in yellow gold, or as an ornament on the neck or head, or as ivory has lustre, set by art in boxwood or Orician terebinth." — Aeneid, x. 134.]

endowed with a singular beauty, and one so excessive that the chastest eyes could not look on its rays chastely. Not content with leaving so much flame and fever wherever he went, with no relief, he turned a furious spite against himself and against those great gifts nature had so generously given him — as if a man were answerable to himself for the sins of others — and deliberately slashed and disfigured, with many wounds and scars, the perfect symmetry and proportion that nature had so carefully imprinted on his face. To give my honest opinion: I admire such actions more than I honour them. These excesses are foreign to my rules. The design was conscientious and good, but a little wanting in prudence. What if his disfigurement later made others guilty of the sin of hatred or contempt; or of envy at the glory of so rare a renunciation; or of slander, interpreting it as mad ambition? Is there any shape that vice cannot, if it will, find some way to put to use? It would have been more just, and also nobler, to make those gifts of God the matter of an exemplary regularity and virtue.

Those who withdraw from the ordinary offices, from that infinite multitude of vexing rules that hamper a man of strict integrity in civil life, are, in my opinion, very prudent — whatever peculiar sharpness of constraint they impose on themselves by doing so. It is in some sense a kind of dying to avoid the pain of living well. They may earn some other reward, but the reward of difficulty I think they can never have; nor, in hardship, can there be anything more or better done than keeping oneself upright in the waves of the world, truly and exactly performing every part of one's duty. It is perhaps easier to keep clear of women altogether than to bear oneself properly in marriage at every point; and a man may with less trouble adapt himself to total abstinence than to the proper management of abundance. Use, conducted according to reason, has more difficulty in it than abstinence; moderation is a virtue that gives more work than mere suffering. Scipio's good living has a thousand variations, Diogenes' has only one; and Diogenes' life surpasses the ordinary ones in innocence as much as Scipio's surpasses them in utility and force.

title: Observation on the means to carry on a war according to Julius Caesar
paragraphs: It is said of many great leaders that they held certain books in special esteem: Alexander the Great, Homer; Scipio Africanus, Xenophon; Marcus Brutus, Polybius; Charles V, Philippe de Commines; and in our day, so they say, Machiavelli still has his following elsewhere. But the late Marshal Strozzi, who had taken Caesar as his man, undoubtedly made the best choice — since Caesar should really be every soldier's breviary, the true and sovereign model of the military art. And, on top of that, God knows with what grace and beauty he has clothed that rich subject, in language so pure, fine, and perfect that, in my opinion, no writings in the world can compare with his on this subject.
I will set down some rare and particular passages from his wars that have stayed in my memory.

When his army was in some panic at the rumour spreading of the great forces King Juba was leading against him, instead of trying to calm his soldiers' fear and play down the enemy's numbers, he called them all together to encourage and reassure them — and took the opposite road from the one we usually take. He told them they need not trouble themselves any further about asking how strong the enemy was, since he was reliably informed of it; and then he named a number that vastly exceeded both the truth and the rumour that was running in his army. He was following Cyrus' advice in Xenophon: it is much less damaging to find an enemy weaker than you expected than to find him really very strong after having been told he was weak.

It was always his practice to train his soldiers simply to obey, without taking it on themselves to pass judgment on, or even talk about, their captain's plans, which he never communicated to them until the very point of execution. He took a pleasure, if they got wind of any of his intentions, in immediately changing his orders to throw them off. For that purpose he would often, after assigning quarters in a place, push on and lengthen his day's march, especially in foul and rainy weather.

When the Swiss, at the start of his wars in Gaul, sent to demand free passage across Roman territory, he was already determined to stop them by force; yet he spoke kindly to their envoys and took some time before answering, in order to use that time to gather his army. Those silly people did not realise what a careful manager he was of his time — for he often repeats that the best part of a captain is to know how to use opportunities, and his speed in his exploits is, in truth, unheard of and incredible.

If he was not very scrupulous about taking advantage of an enemy under cover of a treaty, he was as little scrupulous in another respect: he required no virtue in a soldier but valour, and rarely punished any faults but mutiny and disobedience. He would often, after his victories, turn his men loose to every kind of licence, releasing them for a time from the rules of military discipline — and said that he had soldiers so well trained that, powdered and perfumed, they would still rush furiously to the fight. He liked them to be richly armed, and he gave them engraved, gilt, and damascened armour, so that the care of preserving it would push them to defend it more stubbornly. In speaking to them, he called them "fellow-soldiers," which we still use today; his successor Augustus changed this, supposing Caesar had used the word only out of necessity, and to flatter men who were following him as mere volunteers:
"Rheni mihi Caesar in undis Dux erat; hic socius; facinus quos inquinat, aequat:"
["In the waters of the Rhine Caesar was my general; here at Rome he is my fellow. Crime levels those whom it pollutes." — Lucan, v. 289.]
but this form of address was too low and mean for the dignity of an emperor and general of an army, and so Augustus brought in the custom of simply calling them "soldiers."

With this courtesy Caesar mixed great severity, to keep them in awe. When the ninth legion mutinied near Placentia he discharged them ignominiously, even though Pompey was then still in the field, and only took them back into favour after many entreaties; he quieted them more by authority and boldness than by gentle methods.

Where he speaks of his passage across the Rhine into Germany, he says that he thought it beneath the honour of the Roman people to ferry his army over in boats, and so he built a bridge to let them cross dry-footed. That was the famous bridge he describes in such detail. He never dwells more willingly on his actions than when showing us the ingenuity of his inventions in projects of that sort.

I have noted, too, how much value he set on his exhortations to the soldiers before battle: wherever he wants to show that he was caught off guard or forced into fighting, he always brings in the point that he had no time even to harangue his army. Before that great battle with the people of Tournai: "Caesar," he says, "having given orders for everything else, ran at once where chance led him, to encourage his men; and meeting the tenth legion, had time only to tell them to remember their usual valour, not to be alarmed, and to meet the enemy's onset bravely; and seeing the enemy was already within javelin-range, he gave the signal for battle. Then, going off elsewhere to encourage others, he found they were already engaged." That is what he tells us in that passage. His tongue, in fact, did him notable service on many occasions, and his military eloquence was so highly thought of in his own time that many in his army wrote down his harangues as he spoke them, so that volumes of them were collected that survived long after him. He had so particular a grace in speaking that his close friends — and Augustus among them — could pick out, on hearing the speeches read aloud, even the phrases and words that were not his.

The first time he left Rome on any public command, he reached the Rhone in eight days, with a secretary or two in the coach in front of him constantly writing, and the man carrying his sword behind. And really, even if a man did nothing but travel, he could scarcely match the speed with which Caesar, after being everywhere victorious in Gaul, left it, and, following Pompey to Brundisium, subdued all Italy in eighteen days; returned from Brundisium to Rome; from Rome went into the very heart of Spain, where he overcame extreme difficulties in the war against Afranius and Petreius, and in the long siege of Marseilles; from there he went back into Macedonia, beat the Roman army at Pharsalia, passed in pursuit of Pompey into Egypt, which he also subdued; from Egypt went into Syria and the territories of Pontus, where he fought Pharnaces; from there into Africa, where he defeated Scipio and Juba; returned once again through Italy, where he defeated Pompey's sons:
"Ocyor et coeli fiammis, et tigride foeta."
["Swifter than lightning, or the cub-bearing tigress." — Lucan, v. 405.]

"Ac veluti montis saxum de vertice praeceps Cum ruit avulsum vento, seu turbidus imber Proluit, aut annis solvit sublapsa vetustas, Fertur in abruptum magno mons improbus actu, Exultatque solo, silvas, armenta, virosque, Involvens secum."

["And as a stone torn from the mountain's top by the wind or rain torrents, or loosened by age, falls massive with mighty force, bounds here and there, in its course sweeping from the earth with it woods, herds, and men." — Aeneid, xii. 684.]

Speaking of the siege of Avaricum, he says it was his custom to be with the pioneers night and day. In all enterprises of consequence he reconnoitred in person, and never brought his army into quarters until he had first seen the place; and if we can believe Suetonius, when he resolved to cross into England he was the first man to sound the passage.

He used to say he set more store by a victory won by strategy than by force; and in the war against Petreius and Afranius, when fortune offered him a chance of an obvious advantage, he refused it, saying he hoped, with a little more time but less risk, to overcome his enemies. He also did a notable thing there, ordering his whole army to swim across the river, without any sort of necessity for it:
"Rapuitque ruens in praelia miles, Quod fugiens timuisset, iter; mox uda receptis Membra fovent armis, gelidosque a gurgite, cursu Restituunt artus."

["The soldier rushed through a way to fight which he would have been afraid to take in flight: then, with their armour, they cover wet limbs, and by running restore warmth to their numbed joints." — Lucan, iv. 151.]

I find him a little more temperate and considered in his undertakings than Alexander, who seems to seek out and rush headlong on danger like an impetuous torrent that attacks and crashes against everything it meets, without discrimination or restraint:
"Sic tauriformis volvitur Aufidus; Qui regna Dauni perfluit Appuli, Dum saevit, horrendamque cultis Diluviem meditatur agris;"
["So the bull-shaped Aufidus rolls, which flows through the realm of the Apulian Daunus, when raging, threatens a fearful deluge to the cultivated ground." — Horace, Odes, iv. 14, 25.]

and, indeed, Alexander was a general in the flower and first heat of his youth, whereas Caesar took up the trade at a ripe and well-advanced age. Add to that the fact that Alexander was of a more sanguine, hot, and choleric constitution, which he further inflamed with wine — from which Caesar abstained almost entirely.

But where necessary occasion required, no man ever risked his person more than Caesar did. So much so that, for my part, I seem to read in many of his exploits a settled resolution to throw himself away rather than face the shame of being beaten. In his great battle with the people of Tournai, he charged right up to the head of the enemy without his shield, just as he saw the van of his own army beginning to give ground — and the same thing happened to him several other times. Hearing his people were besieged, he passed through the enemy's army in disguise to encourage them with his presence. Having crossed over to Dyrrachium with very slight forces, and seeing the rest of his army, which he had left to Antony's command, slow to follow him, he set out alone to recross the sea in a tremendous storm, and slipped away in secret to fetch the rest of his troops, with the ports on the other side held by Pompey and the whole sea in his enemy's possession. As for what he accomplished by sheer force of hand, there are many exploits in which the risk goes beyond all the rules of war. With what small means did he undertake to subdue the kingdom of Egypt, and afterwards to attack the forces of Scipio and Juba, ten times greater than his own? These men had I-don't-know-what more-than-human confidence in their fortune; and he used to say that in great undertakings men must embark, not deliberate. After the battle of Pharsalia, when he had sent his army on ahead into Asia and was crossing the Hellespont in a single vessel, he met Lucius Cassius at sea with ten tall warships — and had the courage not only to wait for him but to sail up to him and summon him to surrender, which he did.

When he undertook that furious siege of Alesia, where there were eighty thousand men in garrison, with all Gaul up in arms to raise the siege and a relieving army on foot of one hundred and nine thousand horse and two hundred and forty thousand foot — what boldness and what high confidence it took in him not to give up the attempt but to resolve to face both these enormous difficulties, which he nevertheless overcame; and, after winning that great battle against the army outside, he soon reduced those inside to his mercy. The same thing happened to Lucullus at the siege of Tigranocerta against King Tigranes, but the enemy's quality there was not the same, given the softness of the men Lucullus was dealing with. I will set down here two rare and extraordinary incidents from this siege of Alesia. The first: the Gauls, having mustered their forces against Caesar and made a general review of them, resolved in their council of war to dismiss a good part of that huge multitude, so as not to fall into confusion. This example of fearing to be too many is new; but, properly considered, it stands to reason that the body of an army should be of moderate size and kept within certain bounds, both because of the difficulty of provisioning them and the difficulty of governing them and keeping them in order. At the very least, it is very easy to show by example that monstrously large armies have rarely accomplished anything of substance. As Cyrus says in Xenophon, "It is not the number of men, but the number of good men, that wins the advantage"; the rest only get in the way. And Bayezid based his decision to fight Tamerlane, against the opinion of all his captains, mainly on this — that his enemies' uncountable numbers gave him sure hope of confusion in their ranks. Scanderbeg, a very good and expert judge in such matters, used to say that ten or twelve thousand reliable fighting men were enough for a good leader to keep himself in order in every kind of military situation. The other thing I want to record, which seems contrary to the custom and rules of war, is that Vercingetorix, who was made general of all the parts of the revolted Gaul, went and shut himself up in Alesia. The man who commands a whole country ought never to shut himself up except in such extremity that the only place he has left is in danger, and that his only remaining hope is in the defence of that city; otherwise he should keep himself at liberty, so that he can take general measures for every part of his command.

To return to Caesar. He grew, in time, slower and more considered, as his friend Oppius testifies: thinking he should not lightly hazard the glory of so many victories which one stroke of fortune could take from him. That is what the Italians mean when they want to reproach the rashness and foolhardiness of young people, calling them bisognosi d'onore — "in need of honour" — meaning that, being in such a want and dearth of reputation, they have reason to seek it at any price; which those who have already acquired enough should not do. There may reasonably be some moderation, some satiety, in this thirst and appetite for glory, as in other things; and there are plenty of people who practise it.

He was very far from the religious scruples of the old Romans, who would never prevail in their wars except by sheer pure valour; and yet he was more conscientious than we should be these days, and did not approve of every means to win victory. In the war against Ariovistus, while he was parleying with him, a skirmish broke out among the cavalry, started by the fault of Ariovistus' light horse — and although Caesar saw he had a very great advantage over the enemy at that moment, he would not use it, for fear of being reproached with treacherous dealing.
He always wore rich garments, and of a striking colour, in battle, so as to be more visible and better watched.

He kept a stricter and tighter hand over his soldiers the closer he was to an enemy. When the ancient Greeks wanted to accuse anyone of complete incompetence, they used to say, as a common proverb, that he could neither read nor swim. Caesar was of the same opinion: that swimming was very useful in war, and he himself found it so. When he needed to move fast, he commonly swam across the rivers in his way; he loved to march on foot, as did Alexander the Great. When he was in Egypt and was forced, to save himself, to get into a little boat, and so many men leapt in with him that it was in danger of sinking, he chose rather to trust himself to the sea, and swam to his fleet two hundred paces off, holding his tablets in his left hand and dragging his cloak in his teeth so that it would not fall into the enemy's hands — and at that point in his life he was already fairly far on in years.

Never has any general had such credit with his soldiers. At the start of the civil wars, his centurions offered to find each a man-at-arms at his own expense, and the foot soldiers to serve him at their own cost — and those better off offered, on top of that, to pay for the more necessitous. The late Admiral Chastillon
[Gaspard de Coligny, assassinated in the St Bartholomew massacre, 24 August 1572.]

showed us a similar example in our civil wars; the Frenchmen in his army put up money out of their own purses to pay the foreigners who served with him. Such warm and ready affection among the soldiers of earlier times — who kept strictly to their rules of war — is rarely found in examples; passion has more absolute command over us than reason. And yet it happened, in the war against Hannibal, that following the example of the people of Rome in the city, the soldiers and officers in the army refused their pay, and in Marcellus' camp those who would take any were branded with the name "Mercenaries." Having taken the worst of it near Dyrrachium, Caesar's soldiers came and offered themselves up to be chastised and punished, so that there was more need to comfort than to reprove them. One single cohort of his held off four of Pompey's legions for more than four hours, until they were almost all killed by arrows, so that one hundred and thirty thousand shafts were found in the trenches. A soldier called Scaeva, who held one of the passes, invincibly maintained his position with one eye gone, one shoulder and one thigh shot through, and his shield struck in two hundred and thirty places. It happened that many of his soldiers, when taken prisoner, chose to die rather than promise to go over to the other side. Granius Petronius was taken by Scipio in Africa: Scipio, having put the rest to death, sent him word that he gave him his life, since he was a man of quality and a quaestor. Petronius sent back word that Caesar's soldiers were used to giving others their lives, not to receiving theirs; and immediately killed himself with his own hand.

There are countless examples of their loyalty, but what was done by those besieged in Salona — a city that held out for Caesar against Pompey — must not be forgotten, for the rarity of what happened there. Marcus Octavius was holding them tightly besieged. Inside, they had been reduced to the extreme need of everything: to make up for the lack of men, with most either killed or wounded, they had freed all their slaves; to make ropes for their war-engines they had had to cut off all the women's hair; on top of all this they were starving, and yet they were resolved never to surrender. After the siege had dragged on long enough that Octavius had grown careless and slack in pressing his enterprise, they picked a day about noon, placed the women and children on the walls for show, and sallied out against the besiegers with such fury that they routed the first, second, and third bodies of troops, and then the fourth, and the rest; they beat them clean out of their trenches and chased them right down to their ships. Octavius himself was forced to flee to Dyrrachium, where Pompey lay. I do not at this moment remember another example where the besieged completely defeated the besieger and won the field, or where a sortie produced a pure and total victory.

title: Of three good women
paragraphs: They are not by the dozen, as everyone knows, and especially in the duties of marriage; for marriage is a bargain full of so many delicate clauses that it is hard for a woman's will to bear that restraint for long. Men, though their condition is somewhat better under the same tie, still have enough on their hands. The true test of a happy marriage looks at the time of the companionship: whether it has been steadily gentle, loyal, and agreeable. In our day women commonly hold back the public showing of their good offices, and of their passionate affection for their husbands, until they have lost them — or at least put off the testimonies of their goodwill till then. A slow and untimely testimony. By it they rather demonstrate that they never loved their husbands until they were dead: their life is nothing but trouble, their death full of love and politeness. As fathers conceal their affection from their children, women conceal theirs from their husbands, to maintain a modest decorum. This kind of mystery is not to my taste. They scratch themselves and tear their hair for nothing. I whisper in a waiting-woman's or a secretary's ear: "How were they together, how did they live?" I always have that good saying in my head:
"Jactantius moerent, quae minus dolent."
["They make the greatest show of grief who feel it least." — Tacitus, Annals, ii. 77, writing of Germanicus.]

Their wailing is offensive to the living and useless to the dead. We would willingly let them laugh once we are gone, provided they smile on us while we are alive. Is it not enough to make a man revive in pure spite — that she who spat in my face while I was alive should come and kiss my feet once I am dead? If there is any honour in mourning a husband, it belongs only to those who smiled on them while they had them; let those who wept during their lives laugh at their deaths, outwardly as well as inwardly. So never mind the puffy red eyes and the pitiful voice; look at her bearing, her colour, the plumpness of her cheeks under all those formal veils — that is where she speaks plain French. There are few who do not improve on it, and good health cannot lie. That starched and ceremonious expression looks not so much back as forward, and is meant rather to find a new husband than to mourn the old. When I was a boy, a very beautiful and virtuous lady, who is still alive, the widow of a prince, wore a little more ornament in her dress than our laws of widowhood allow; when she was reproached for it she answered that it was because she was resolved never again to have any love affair, and would never marry again.

I have here, not at all in opposition to our customs, picked out three women who likewise showed the utmost goodness and affection at the deaths of their husbands; but they are examples of a kind no longer in use, and so severe that they will hardly be drawn into imitation.

The younger Pliny had near a house of his in Italy a neighbour who was being tormented by certain ulcers on his private parts. His wife, seeing him drag on so long, asked him to let her examine the state of his disease at leisure, and to tell him frankly what she thought. He gave permission, and she, having looked carefully into the matter, found it impossible he could ever be cured: all he had to hope for was a long lingering, painful and miserable life. So, as the most sure and sovereign remedy, she calmly advised him to kill himself. But finding him a little tender and reluctant in so harsh an undertaking, she said, "Do not think, my dear, that the torments I see you in are not as keenly felt by me as by you, and that to deliver myself from them I will not myself use the same remedy I have prescribed for you. I will keep you company in the cure as I have done in the disease. Fear nothing — believe that we shall take pleasure in this passage, which is to free us from so many miseries; and we will go together happily." Having said that, and put fresh courage into her husband, she resolved that they should throw themselves headlong into the sea from a window that overlooked it. And so as to keep up to the last the loyal and passionate affection with which she had embraced him in his life, she wanted him to die in her arms as well — but lest they should let go of each other in the fall from fear, she bound herself fast to him at the waist, and so gave her own life to procure her husband's rest. This was a woman of low condition; and among that class of people it is no very new thing to see examples of rare virtue:
"Extrema per illos Justitia excedens terris vestigia fecit."
["Justice, when she left the earth, took her last steps among them." — Virgil, Georgics, ii. 473.]
The other two were noble and rich, and examples of virtue are seldom lodged there.

Arria, the wife of Caecina Paetus, a man of consular rank, was the mother of another Arria, the wife of Thrasea Paetus — the same Thrasea whose virtue was so celebrated in Nero's time — and through this son-in-law she was the grandmother of Fannia (the resemblance of these men's and women's names, and of their fortunes, has led to several confusions). This first Arria, when her husband Caecina Paetus had been captured by some of the Emperor Claudius' men after the defeat of Scribonianus — whose party he had embraced in the war — begged those who were to carry him prisoner to Rome to take her along on their ship, where she would be much less expense and trouble to them than the many attendants they would otherwise have to maintain to wait on her husband, and that she alone would undertake to look after him in his room, his kitchen, and every other office. They refused. So she put herself into a fisherman's boat she hired on the spot, and in that way followed him from Illyria. After her arrival at Rome, Junia, the widow of Scribonianus, one day, on the strength of their similar fortunes, came up to her in the Emperor's presence; Arria pushed her off roughly with these words: "I," she said, "speak to you, or listen to anything you have to say! — to you, in whose lap Scribonianus was killed, and you are still alive?" These words, with several other signs, made her friends realise she would certainly take her own life, unable to endure her husband's misfortune. And Thrasea, her son-in-law, begging her not to throw herself away, and saying to her, "What — if I should suffer the same fate as Caecina, would you want your daughter, my wife, to do the same?" — "Would I?" she replied. "Yes, yes, I would: if she had lived as long, and in as good understanding with you, as I have lived with my husband." These answers made them all the more careful of her, and more watchful in their eye on her. One day, when she said to those guarding her, "You take all this trouble for nothing; you may indeed make me die a worse death, but to keep me from dying is not in your power" — she suddenly leapt from a chair where she had been sitting and with all her strength dashed her head against the wall, by which blow she was knocked flat in a faint and badly wounded. After they had with great difficulty brought her back to herself, she said, "I told you that if you denied me some easy way of dying, I would find another, however painful." The conclusion of so admirable a virtue was this. Her husband Paetus, not having resolution enough of his own to despatch himself as the emperor's cruelty had ordered him to, one day, after she had used all the reasons and exhortations she thought most likely to persuade him, she snatched the dagger he wore at his side, held it ready in her hand to clinch her admonitions, and saying "Do this, Paetus," in the same instant gave herself a mortal stab in the breast, then drew it out of the wound and presented it to him, ending her life with this noble, generous, and immortal saying — "Paete, non dolet" — having time to pronounce no more than those three never-to-be-forgotten words: "Paetus, it does not hurt."
"Casta suo gladium cum traderet Arria Paeto, Quem de visceribus traxerat ipsa suis Si qua fides, vulnus quod feci non dolet, inquit, Sed quod tu facies, id mihi, Paete, dolet."

["When the chaste Arria gave to Paetus the reeking sword she had drawn from her own breast, 'If you believe me,' she said, 'Paetus, the wound I have made does not hurt; it is the one you will make, Paetus, that hurts me.'" — Martial, i. 14.]

The action was nobler in itself, and of a braver sense, than the poet expressed it. So far from being deterred by the thought of her husband's wound, his death, and her own, she had been the one to propose them and urge them; but having performed this high and courageous undertaking solely for her husband's sake, she was thinking, even in the last gasp of her life, only of him — of relieving him of the fear of dying along with her. Paetus at once stabbed himself to the heart with the same weapon, ashamed, I suppose, to have needed so dear and precious an example.

Pompeia Paulina, a young and very noble Roman lady, had married Seneca in his extreme old age. Nero, his fine pupil, sent his guards to him to deliver the death-sentence, which was carried out in this fashion: when the Roman emperors of those days had condemned a man of rank, they sent word by their officers to him to choose his manner of death, and to carry it out within such or such a time-limit, which was set, depending on the degree of their anger, either shorter or longer, so as to give him time to put his affairs in order — or sometimes to deny him even that, by the shortness of the period. If the condemned man seemed unwilling to obey the order, they had men ready to carry it out either by cutting the veins of his arms and legs, or by forcing him to swallow a dose of poison. But men of honour would not submit to that necessity, but called in their own doctors and surgeons for the job. Seneca, with a calm and steady face, heard their charge and at once called for paper to make his will. When the captain refused him this, he turned to his friends and said, "Since I am not allowed to leave you any other token of the debt I owe you, I leave you at least the best thing I have, namely the image of my life and conduct, which I beg you to keep in memory of me — and by doing so you will earn the glory of sincere and real friends." Then, one moment soothing with gentle words the grief he saw in them, the next raising his voice to rebuke them: "What," he said, "has become of all our fine philosophical maxims? What of all the provisions we have laid in for so many years against the strokes of fortune? Is Nero's cruelty unknown to us? What could we expect of one who has murdered his mother and his brother, but that he should put to death the tutor who brought him up?" After those general words, he turned to his wife and embraced her tightly in his arms, as, her heart and strength failing her, she was ready to sink down with grief; and he begged her, for his sake, to bear this stroke with a little more patience, telling her that the hour had come in which he was to show, not by argument and discourse but in action, the fruit he had reaped from his studies, and that he genuinely embraced his death, not only without grief but with joy. "And so, my dearest," he said, "do not dishonour it with your tears, lest it look as if you loved yourself more than my reputation. Restrain your grief, and console yourself in what you have known of me and of my actions, leading the rest of your life in the same virtuous way you have done up to now." Paulina, having recovered her spirits a little, and warmed the greatness of her courage with a most generous affection, replied: "No, Seneca, I am not a woman to let you go alone in such a moment. I will not have you think that the virtuous examples of your life have not taught me how to die; and when could I ever do it better, or more fittingly, or more as I would wish, than with you? So be sure: I will go along with you." Then Seneca, taking this noble and generous resolution of his wife in good part, and willing also to free himself from the fear of leaving her exposed to his enemies' cruelty after his death, said, "Paulina, I have instructed you in what would serve you for a happy life; but you, I see, are more set on the honour of dying. Truly, I will not grudge it to you. The steadiness and resolve in our common end are the same; but the beauty and glory of your part are much greater." That said, the surgeons at the same moment opened the veins of both their arms; but as Seneca's, more shrunken with age and abstinence, let his blood flow too slowly, he further ordered them to open the veins of his thighs. And so that the torments he was suffering might not pierce his wife's heart, and also to spare himself the affliction of seeing her in so sad a state, after a very affectionate farewell he begged her to allow them to carry her into her own room, which they did. But all these incisions still being not enough to make him die, he ordered Statius Annaeus, his physician, to give him a draught of poison, which had not much better effect — because of the weakness and coldness of his limbs it could not reach his heart. So they were forced to add a very hot bath; and then, feeling his end approach, while he still had breath he kept up admirable discourse on the subject of his present condition, which his secretaries took down as long as they could hear him; and his last words long remained in great honour and esteem among men, and it is a great loss to us that they have not come down to our day. Then, feeling the last pangs of death, with the bloody water of the bath he bathed his head and said, "This water I dedicate to Jupiter the Deliverer." Nero, hearing of all this at once, and fearing that the death of Paulina — who was one of the best-born ladies of Rome, and against whom he had no particular grudge — would turn into a reproach against him, sent orders in all haste to bind up her wounds. Her attendants did so without her knowledge, since she was already half dead and quite past all sensation. So although she lived against her own design, she lived very honourably, in a way befitting her own virtue, and her pale complexion afterwards bore continual witness to how much life had run out of her veins.

These are my three quite true stories, which I find as entertaining and as tragic as any of those we make up out of our own heads to amuse the common people. And I wonder why those who give themselves to such writing do not rather pick out ten thousand very fine stories which are to be found in books, which would save them the trouble of invention, and would be more useful and entertaining. Anyone who wanted to put a whole, connected body of them together would need to add nothing of his own but the joining — the solder of another metal, as it were — and might in that way assemble a great many true events of every kind, ordering and varying them according as the beauty of the work required, much as Ovid has built his Metamorphoses out of the endless number of his various fables.

In the last pair, there is moreover this to consider: that Paulina voluntarily offered to lose her life out of love of her husband, and that her husband had earlier refrained from dying out of love of her. We may think there is no fair counterbalance in this exchange; but, in his Stoic way, I take it he thought he had done as much for her by prolonging his life on her account as if he had died for her. In one of his letters to Lucilius, after letting him know that, struck down by a fever in Rome, he had at once taken his coach to head for a house of his in the country, against his wife's wish, who wanted him to stay — and that he had told her the fever he was struck with was not a fever of the body but of the place — he goes on: "She let me go," he says, "with strict orders to look after my health. Now I, knowing that her life is bound up in mine, am beginning to make much of myself, so that I can preserve her. And I lose the privilege my age has given me of being more steady and resolute in many things, when I remember that in this old fellow there is a young girl whose interests are tied to his health. And since I cannot persuade her to love me more bravely, she makes me love myself more solicitously. We must allow something to honourable affections; sometimes, even when occasions urge us the other way, we must call life back, even with pain; we must hold the soul fast in our teeth, since the rule of life for good men is not as long as they please but as long as they should. He who does not love his wife or his friend enough to prolong his life for them, but is set on dying, is too dainty and too soft. The soul must lay this duty on itself, when our friends' need requires it; we must sometimes lend ourselves to our friends, and break our resolve to die for ourselves on their behalf. It is a mark of greatness of courage to come back to life out of consideration for another, as many excellent men have done; and it is a mark of singular good nature to preserve old age — of which the chief convenience is indifference to its length and a stout, disdainful use of life — when a man sees that doing so is pleasant, agreeable, and useful to someone who loves him very much. And one reaps a very pleasing reward in it; for what can be more delightful than to be so dear to one's wife that on her account one becomes dearer to oneself? So my Paulina has loaded me not only with her fears but with my own; it has not been enough for me to consider how resolutely I could die — I have also had to consider how irresolutely she would bear my death. I am compelled to live, and sometimes to live in greatness of spirit." These are his own words, as excellent as they everywhere are.

title: Of the most excellent men
paragraphs: If I were asked which men, of all I have come across, I would pick, I should answer that, to my mind, I find three I rank above the rest.

One is Homer. Not that Aristotle or Varro, for example, were not perhaps as learned as he was; nor that Virgil was not his equal in his own art — that I leave to those who know them both to settle. I, who only really understand one of them, can only say this, by my poor lights: that I do not believe the Muses themselves could ever go beyond the Roman:
"Tale facit carmen docta testudine, quale Cynthius impositis temperat articulis:"
["He plays on his learned lyre a verse such as Cynthian Apollo modulates with his imposed fingers." — Propertius, ii. 34, 79.]

and yet, when we say this, we must not forget that it is mainly from Homer that Virgil draws his excellence — that Homer is his guide and teacher, and that one stroke of the Iliad gave him the body and matter from which to put together his great and divine Aeneid. But that is not all I am reckoning with: I add several other circumstances that make this poet seem to me admirable, almost beyond human condition. And, in truth, I often wonder that the man who produced — and gave their place in the world to — so many gods was not made a god himself. Blind and poor, living before the sciences had been put into rule and definite observation, he knew them so well that all who have since undertaken to set up governments, to wage wars, or to write either about religion or about philosophy, of whatever sect, or about the arts, have used him as the most perfect instructor in every kind of knowledge, and his books as a treasury of every sort of learning:
"Qui, quid sit pulcrum, quid turpe, quid utile, quid non, Planius ac melius Chrysippo et Crantore dicit:"
["Who tells us what is fair, what foul, what useful, what not, more clearly and better than Chrysippus and Crantor?" — Horace, Epistles, i. 2, 3.]
and, as another says,
"A quo, ceu fonte perenni, Vatum Pieriis ora rigantur aquis"
["From whom, as from a perennial spring, the lips of poets are moistened with Pierian waters." — Ovid, Amores, iii. 9, 25.]
and another,
"Adde Heliconiadum comites, quorum unus Homerus Sceptra potitus;"
["Add the companions of the Muses, of whom Homer alone has won the sceptre." — Lucretius, iii. 1050.]
and another:
"Cujusque ex ore profusos Omnis posteritas latices in carmina duxit, Amnemque in tenues ausa est deducere rivos. Unius foecunda bonis."

["From whose mouth all posterity has drawn copious streams of verse, and has dared to channel the mighty river into its little rivulets, fertile in the wealth of one man." — Manilius, Astronomica, ii. 8.]

It is against the order of nature that he should have made the most excellent thing that can be made; for the ordinary birth of things is imperfect — they grow and gather strength by growing — whereas he made the infancy of poetry and of several other sciences mature, perfect, and complete at the outset. For that reason he can be called the first and last of poets, in keeping with the fine testimony antiquity has left of him: "as there was no one before him whom he could imitate, so there has been no one since who could imitate him." His words, according to Aristotle, are the only words that have motion and action, the only substantial words. Alexander the Great, having found a rich casket among Darius' spoils, ordered it be set aside to keep his Homer in, saying that Homer was the best and most faithful counsellor he had in his military affairs. For the same reason Cleomenes, son of Anaxandridas, said that Homer was the poet of the Spartans, as being an excellent master of the discipline of war. There is also this singular tribute to him in Plutarch's judgment: that he is the only author in the world who never glutted or sickened his readers, always presenting himself as something new, and always flourishing in some fresh grace. That naughty Alcibiades, asking one who pretended to learning for a book of Homer, gave him a box on the ear because he had none — which he thought as scandalous as we should if we found one of our priests without a breviary. Xenophanes complained one day to Hiero, tyrant of Syracuse, that he was so poor he could not afford to keep two servants. "What!" Hiero replied. "Homer, who was much poorer than you, keeps more than ten thousand, though he is dead." What did Panaetius leave unsaid when he called Plato the Homer of the philosophers? Besides, what glory can be compared to his? Nothing is more constantly on men's lips than his name and works; nothing is so well known and accepted as Troy, Helen, and the war fought over her — when perhaps there never was such a thing. Our children are still called by names he invented more than three thousand years ago; who does not know Hector and Achilles? Not only certain particular families but most nations also trace their origins to his inventions. Mehmed II, emperor of the Turks, writing to our Pope Pius II, said, "I am astonished the Italians take up arms against me, considering we share a common descent from the Trojans, and it is just as much my business as theirs to revenge the blood of Hector on the Greeks, whom they side with against me." Is it not a noble farce, in which kings, republics, and emperors have played their parts for so many ages, with the vast universe for a stage? Seven Greek cities contended for the honour of being his birthplace — so much honour even his obscurity helped him to:
"Smyrna, Rhodos, Colophon, Salamis, Chios, Argos, Athenae."

The second is Alexander the Great. Consider the age at which he began his undertakings; the small means by which he carried out so dazzling a design; the authority he won, in his mere youth, with the greatest and most experienced captains in the world, who followed him; the extraordinary favour with which fortune embraced and protected so many hazardous — not to say reckless — exploits;
"Impellens quicquid sibi summa petenti Obstaret, gaudensque viam fecisse ruina;"
["Bearing down all who stood between him and the heights he sought, and pleased to force his way by ruin." — Lucan, i. 149.]

that greatness, by which at the age of thirty-three he had passed victorious through the whole habitable earth and, in half a life, reached the very limit of what human nature can achieve — so that you cannot imagine what his proper span and the continued growth of his courage and fortune would have been, had he reached due maturity of age, without imagining something more than human. Consider the many royal lines he made spring from his soldiers, leaving the world, at his death, divided among four successors — simple captains in his army — whose posterity so long held and maintained that vast inheritance. Consider so many excellent virtues he was master of: justice, temperance, generosity, truth in his word, love towards his own people, humanity towards those he overcame. His character, in general, seems incapable of any sort of reproach — though some particular and exceptional actions of his may fall under censure. But it is impossible to carry off such great things as he did within the strict rules of justice; such men are to be judged in the gross, by the main end of their actions. The destruction of Thebes and Persepolis, the murder of Menander and of Hephaestion's physician, the massacre of so many Persian prisoners at one time, of a body of Indian soldiers (not without breaking his word), and of the Cossaeans down to the children themselves, are indeed lapses not easily excused. As for Cleitus, the fault was more than redeemed; and that action, as much as any other, displays the goodness of his nature, a nature most exquisitely formed for good. It was ingeniously said of him that he had his virtues from nature and his vices from fortune. As for his being a little given to bragging, a little too impatient of hearing himself ill spoken of, and as for those mangers, weapons, and bits he had scattered about in India — all those little vanities, it seems to me, can well be allowed to his youth and to the prodigious good fortune that attended him. And anyone who will set against them his many military virtues — his diligence, foresight, patience, discipline, subtlety, magnanimity, resolution, and good luck (in which, even without Hannibal's testimony, he stood first among men) — the admirable beauty and symmetry of his person, miraculous to the point of seeming a miracle, his stately bearing and awesome look, in a face so young, ruddy, and radiant:
"Qualis, ubi Oceani perfusus Lucifer unda, Quem Venus ante alios astrorum diligit ignes, Extulit os sacrum coelo, tenebrasque resolvit;"
["As when, bathed in the waves of Ocean, Lucifer, whom Venus loves beyond the other fires of stars, lifts his sacred face to heaven and dispels the darkness." — Aeneid, iii. 589.]

the excellence of his knowledge and capacity; the length and grandeur of his glory, pure and clean, without spot or envy; the fact that long after his death it was a religious belief that even his medallions brought good fortune to those who wore them; and that more kings and princes have written about his actions than other historians have written about the actions of any other king or prince — and that even today the Mohammedans, who despise all other histories, accept and honour his alone by a special privilege: whoever, I say, will seriously consider all this will agree that, taking everything together, I had reason to set him above Caesar himself, the only one who could make me hesitate in my choice. And it cannot be denied that there was more of him in his own exploits, and more of fortune in those of Alexander. They were equal in many things, and perhaps Caesar had some greater qualities. They were two fires, two torrents, sweeping over the world by different ways:

"Ac velut immissi diversis partibus ignes Arentem in silvam, et virgulta sonantia lauro Aut ubi decursu rapido de montibus altis Dant sonitum spumosi amnes, et in aequora currunt, Quisque suum populatus iter:"

["And as fires set in different parts of a dry wood and crackling laurel shrubs, or as foaming torrents pour down from the high mountains in headlong descent and rush to the sea, each ravaging its own course." — Aeneid, xii. 521.]

but even had Caesar's ambition been more moderate, it would still be so unhappy, having the ruin of his country and the universal mischief of the world for its abominable object, that, all things put together and weighed in the balance, I must come down on Alexander's side.

The third, and in my opinion the most excellent, is Epaminondas. Of glory he has nowhere near so much as the other two (which, for that matter, is only a part of the substance of the thing); of valour and resolve — not the kind driven by ambition but the kind that wisdom and reason can plant in a well-ordered soul — he had all that could be imagined. He has, to my mind, given as ample proof of that virtue as Alexander or Caesar themselves: for although his warlike exploits were neither as frequent nor as imposing, they were, if duly weighed in all their circumstances, just as important, just as bravely fought, and carried with them as clear a testimony of valour and military skill as anyone's. The Greeks have, without dispute, done him the honour of pronouncing him the greatest man of their nation; and to be first in Greece is easily to be first in the world. As to his knowledge, we have this ancient verdict on him, "that no man ever knew so much and spoke so little as he" — for he belonged to the Pythagorean sect. But when he did speak, no one ever spoke better; an excellent orator, and a powerful persuader. But as to his character and conscience, he infinitely surpassed all men who ever undertook the conduct of affairs. For in this one thing — which ought above all to be considered, and which alone really shows what we are, and which alone, I think, outweighs all the rest put together — he comes no way short of any philosopher whatever, not even of Socrates himself. Innocence in this man is a quality peculiar, sovereign, constant, uniform, incorruptible; compared with which it appears in Alexander as subordinate, uncertain, variable, soft, and accidental.
