["That is not a middle way but no way — to wait on events, and pin their decisions on what fortune decides." — Livy, xxxii. 21.]

This may be allowed in our neighbours' affairs; and so Gelo, the tyrant of Syracuse, suspended his choice in the war between the Greeks and the barbarians, keeping a resident ambassador with gifts at Delphi to watch which way fortune would lean, and then take the right moment to join the winners. But it would be a kind of treason to behave that way in our own domestic affairs, where a man must of necessity be on one side or the other. Still, for someone with no office or express command to call him out, sitting still I hold more excusable (and yet I don't excuse myself on those terms) than in foreign expeditions, to which, by our laws, no one is conscripted against his will. And even those who throw themselves wholly into such a war can conduct themselves with such restraint and moderation that the storm may pass over their heads without harming them. Hadn't we reason to hope for such an outcome in the person of the late Bishop of Orléans, the Sieur de Morvilliers?
[An able negotiator who, though protected by the Guises and strongly supporting them, was nevertheless very far from persecuting the Reformers. He died in 1577.]

And I know, among those who carry themselves most bravely in the present war, some whose manners are so gentle, obliging, and just that they will surely stand firm whatever outcome heaven is preparing for us. I am of the opinion that it properly belongs only to kings to quarrel with kings, and I laugh at those spirits who, out of lightness of heart, lend themselves to such ill-matched disputes. A man does not have any more particular quarrel with a prince by marching openly and boldly against him for his own honour and according to his duty; if he doesn't love such a person, he does better — he respects him. And the cause of the laws and of the ancient government of a kingdom in particular has this peculiarity attached: that even those who, for their own private ends, attack them still excuse, if they don't honour, those who defend them.

But we should not, as we now do, call peevishness and inward discontent springing from private interest and passion "duty", nor name a treacherous and malicious course of action "courage". They call their itch for mischief and violence "zeal"; it is not the cause but their own interest that inflames them; they light and start a war not because it is just, but because it is war.

One can very well behave usefully and loyally even among those of the opposing party; carry yourself, if not with equal affection (since that admits of different degrees), at least with an affection moderate, well-tempered, and not so binding to one side that it may demand from you all you are able to do for it — content yourself with a moderate share of their favour and goodwill, and swim in troubled waters without fishing in them.

The other approach — offering yourself and the utmost service you can give to both sides at once — has even less prudence in it than conscience. Doesn't the man to whom you betray someone (to whom you were as welcome as to himself) know that at another time you will do as much for him? He takes you for a villain; meanwhile he listens to what you have to say, gathers intelligence from you, and turns your disloyalty to his own advantage. Double-dealers are useful for bringing things in, but you have to be careful that they carry out as little as possible.

I say nothing to one party that I cannot, if need be, say to the other with a small change of tone; and I report nothing but things either indifferent, or already known, or of common consequence. I cannot allow myself, on any consideration, to tell them a lie. What is entrusted to my secrecy I religiously conceal; but I take on as few such trusts as I can. The secrets of princes are a troublesome burden to anyone with no stake in them. I am very willing to bargain that they trust me with little but rely confidently on what I tell them. I have always known more than I wanted to. One open way of speaking draws out another, and pulls out confidences, like wine and love. Philippides, in my opinion, answered King Lysimachus very well: asked what part of his estate he would like as a gift, he said, "Whatever you wish, so long as it is none of your secrets." I see that everyone is displeased if the bottom of the business he is employed in is hidden from him, or if there is any reservation in the matter; for my part, I am happy to know no more of the business than what they want me to handle, and I have no desire that my knowledge should exceed or fall short of what I have to say. If I must serve as an instrument of deceit, let it be at least with a clear conscience. I will not be considered so devoted or so loyal a servant as to be fit to betray anyone: someone who is unfaithful to himself may be excusably so to his master. But these are princes who don't accept men by halves and despise limited and conditional services: I can't help it; I tell them frankly how far I can go. For I should be a slave to nothing but reason, and I can hardly submit even to that. And they are to blame too for demanding from a free man the same subjection and obligation to their service as they get from someone they have made or bought, or whose fortune particularly and explicitly depends on theirs. The laws have delivered me from a great anxiety; they have chosen a side for me and given me a master; every other allegiance or obligation must be subordinate to that one, and cut off from it. Yet this is not to say that if my affection should incline me otherwise, my hand would at once obey it; the will and desire are a law to themselves, but actions must be commissioned by public appointment.

This whole way of proceeding of mine is a little out of step with the usual forms; it would produce no great effects, nor last for long; innocence itself, in this age of ours, could neither negotiate without dissembling nor trade without lying — and in any case, public employments are by no means to my taste. What my profession requires, I perform in the most private way I can. As a young man I was engaged in business up to the ears, and it went well; but I disengaged in good time. I have often since avoided getting involved, rarely accepted a charge, and never asked for one — keeping my back turned to ambition; not, like rowers, advancing backwards, but at least in such a way that I owe my detachment less to my resolution than to my good fortune in never being fully embarked. For there are paths less displeasing to my taste, and more suited to my abilities, that I would have followed, in spite of all my arguments to the contrary, if fortune had once called me to public service and to advancement in the world's eyes. Those who say, in contradiction to what I profess, that what I call freedom, simplicity, and plainness in my manners is in fact art and subtlety, prudence rather than goodness, calculation rather than nature, good sense rather than good luck — they do me more honour than dishonour. But they are certainly making my subtlety too subtle; and whoever has followed me close and pried into me carefully, I'll give him the victory if he doesn't confess that no rule in their school could match this natural movement, or maintain an appearance of freedom and licence so even and inflexible through so many crooked paths — and that all their cunning and effort could never have steered them through. The way of truth is one and simple; that of private profit, and of the business one is entrusted with, is double, uneven, and shifting. I have often seen these counterfeit and artificial freedoms practised, mostly without success; they remind me of Aesop's ass, who in imitation of the dog kindly clapped his two forefeet on his master's shoulders — but for every caress the dog got for the same display of affection, the poor ass got twice as many blows with a stick for his compliment:
"Id maxime quemque decet, quod est cujusque suum maxime."
["What best becomes each man is what is most his own." — Cicero, De Offic., i. 31.]

I will not deny deceit its due; that would be misunderstanding the world. I know it has often been of great use, and that it keeps most men's employment going. There are vices that are lawful, just as there are many actions, good or excusable, that are not lawful in themselves.
The justice that is in itself natural and universal is otherwise and more nobly ordered than that other justice, which is particular, national, and constrained by the ends of government,
"Veri juris germanaeque justitiae solidam et expressam effigiem nullam tenemus; umbra et imaginibus utimur;"
["We hold no solid and clear image of true right and genuine justice; we use only the shadow and likeness of it." — Cicero, De Offic., iii. 17.]

— so much so that the sage Dandamis, hearing the lives of Socrates, Pythagoras, and Diogenes read aloud, judged them great men in every way except that they were too much subjected to the reverence of the laws, which true virtue, in order to second and authorize them, must give up much of its original vigour for. Many vicious actions are introduced not only by their permission but by their advice:
"Ex senatus consultis plebisquescitis scelera exercentur."
["Crimes are committed by decrees of the Senate and the popular assembly." — Seneca, Ep., 95.]
I follow the common phrase that distinguishes between profitable and honest things, so as to call some natural actions, which are not only profitable but necessary, dishonest and foul.

But let us continue with our examples of treachery. Two claimants to the throne of Thrace had fallen into a dispute about their title; the emperor stopped them from coming to blows. But one of them, under pretext of bringing things to a friendly resolution by an interview, invited his competitor to dine at his own house, imprisoned him, and killed him. Justice required that the Romans get satisfaction for this offence; but there was a difficulty in obtaining it by ordinary means. So what they could not do legitimately, without war and without risk, they decided to do by treachery; what they could not honestly do, they did profitably. To that end one Pomponius Flaccus was found a suitable instrument. By smooth words and assurances he drew the other into his net; and instead of the honour and favour he had promised him, he sent him to Rome bound hand and foot. Here was one traitor betraying another, against common custom: traitors are full of distrust, and it is hard to catch them in their own art — witness the sad experience we have had recently.

Let whoever wants to be Pomponius Flaccus be one — there are plenty who would. For my part, both my word and my faith are, like everything else, parts of this common body: their best effect is the public service, that I take as given. But should someone order me to take charge of law courts and lawsuits, I'd answer that I don't understand the business; or of being a leader of pioneers, I'd say I had been called to a more honourable employment. So also, anyone who wanted to employ me to lie, betray, and perjure myself — though not to assassinate or poison — for some notable service, I would say, "If I have robbed or stolen anything from anyone, send me rather to the galleys." For it is permissible for a man of honour to say, as the Lacedaemonians did when they had been defeated by Antipater and were on the point of concluding terms: "You may impose taxes on us as heavy and ruinous as you please, but if you order us to do shameful and dishonest things, you will waste your time, for it is no use." Everyone should make the same vow to himself that the kings of Egypt made their judges swear solemnly — that they would not do anything against their consciences, no matter how strongly commanded to it by the kings themselves. In such commissions there is an evident mark of disgrace and condemnation; and whoever gives one is at the same time accusing you and giving it to you, if you understand it rightly, as a burden and a punishment. The better the public business is served by your exploit, the worse off you are yourself; and the better you behave in it, the worse for you. And it will be no new thing — nor, perhaps, without some colour of justice — if the very person who set you on then ruins you for it.

If treachery can ever be excusable, it must only be when it is practised to chastise and betray treachery itself. There are plenty of examples of treacheries not only rejected but punished by those they were undertaken for. Who hasn't heard of Fabricius' sentence on the physician of Pyrrhus?

But we also find this on record: that some people who ordered a thing have afterward severely punished the one they employed to carry it out, refusing the reputation of so unbridled an authority and disowning so abandoned and base a servitude and obedience. Jaropelk, Duke of Russia, tempted a Hungarian gentleman to betray Boleslaus, King of Poland, either by killing him or by giving the Russians an opportunity to do him some serious harm. The fellow set about it skilfully: he became more diligent than before in the king's service, so as to obtain the honour of being on his council and one of his chief confidants. With these advantages, and taking the chance of his master's absence, he betrayed Vislicza — a large and rich city — to the Russians, which was entirely sacked and burned, with not only all the inhabitants of both sexes, young and old, put to the sword, but moreover a great number of neighbouring gentry whom he had lured there for that purpose. Jaropelk, his revenge satisfied and his anger appeased (which was not, in fact, without grounds, for Boleslaus had grievously offended him in the same fashion), and sated with the fruit of this treachery, came to consider its enormity with sound judgment and clear of passion. He looked at what had been done with such horror and remorse that he had the eyes bored out and the tongue and shameful parts cut off of the man who had carried it out.

Antigonus persuaded the Argyraspides to betray Eumenes, their general and his enemy, into his hands; but after he had had him put to death once delivered, he chose to make himself the commissioner of divine justice for the punishment of so detestable a crime, and committed the betrayers into the hands of the governor of the province, with express orders to destroy them all by whatever means and bring them to an evil end. So that out of that great number of men, not one ever returned to Macedonia. The better he had been served, the more wickedly he judged the service done, deserving greater punishment.

The slave who betrayed the place where his master, P. Sulpicius, was hiding was, according to Sulla's proscription, freed for his pains; but according to the requirement of public justice, which was bound by no such promise, he was thrown headlong from the Tarpeian rock.

Our King Clovis, instead of the golden arms he had promised them, had three of Cararie's servants hanged after they betrayed their master to him — even though he had been the one who corrupted them. He hanged them with the purse of their reward around their necks: having satisfied his second and special faith, he satisfied the general and first.

Mohammed II, having resolved to be rid of his brother out of state jealousy, according to the practice of the Ottoman family, employed one of his officers to carry out the execution; the man poured water into the brother's mouth so fast that he choked him. This done, to expiate the murder Mohammed handed the murderer over to the mother of the victim — for they were brothers only on the father's side. She, in his presence, ripped open the murderer's chest, rummaged in it with her own hands for his heart, tore it out, and threw it to the dogs. And to even the worst sort of people, nothing is sweeter than, having once secured their end by some vicious act, smuggling some show of virtue and justice into it after the fact, as a kind of compensation and conscientious correction. To which one may add that they look on the ministers of such horrid crimes as men who reproach them with their crimes, and they think to wipe out the memory and testimony of such proceedings by killing those instruments.

Or perhaps you are rewarded so as not to frustrate the public's need for that extreme and desperate remedy. Even so, whoever does the rewarding — if he is not such a man himself — cannot help but look on you as a cursed and execrable fellow, and conclude you a greater traitor than the one against whom you are so. For he reads the malignity of your nature by your own hands, where he cannot possibly be mistaken; you had no prior hatred of the victim to drive you to such an act. He uses you the way they use condemned criminals in executions of justice: an office as necessary as it is dishonourable. Besides the baseness of such commissions, there is also a prostitution of conscience. Because the daughter of Sejanus could not by Roman law be put to death — she was a virgin — to make it legal she was first raped by the executioner and then strangled. Not only his hand but his soul was slave to the public convenience.

When Amurath I, the more grievously to punish his subjects who had taken part in the parricidal rebellion of his son, ordered that the criminals' nearest relatives should assist in the execution, I find it very fine in some of them to have chosen rather to be unjustly thought guilty of someone else's parricide than to serve justice by committing parricide of their own. And where I have seen, at the storming of some small fort in my day, a few wretches who, to save their own skins, agreed to hang their friends and companions, I have thought them in worse condition than those they hanged. It is said that Witold, Prince of Lithuania, brought into use the practice that a criminal condemned to death should execute the sentence with his own hand, thinking it odd that a third person, innocent of the offence, should be made guilty of homicide.

When a prince, under some urgent circumstance or some sudden and unforeseen accident that crucially concerns his state, is compelled to break his word and forfeit his faith, or is forced from his ordinary duty, he should attribute this necessity to a stroke of the divine rod: it is not vice, since he has given up his own reason to a more universal and powerful reason; but it is certainly a misfortune. So that if anyone asks me what remedy there is, "None," I say, "if he was really racked between these two extremes: 'sed videat, ne quoeratur latebra perjurio' — he had to do it. But if he did it without regret, if it did not weigh on him to do it, that is a sign his conscience is in a sorry state." If a man could be found of so tender a conscience that he could think no cure whatever worth so important a remedy, I should think none the worse of him; he could not perish more excusably or more becomingly. We cannot do everything we would; so we must often, as a last anchorage, commit the protection of our vessel to the simple guidance of heaven. To what more just necessity does he hold himself in reserve? What is more impossible for him to do than what he cannot do without giving up his faith and honour — things that, perhaps, ought to be dearer to him than his own safety, or even the safety of his people? Even if he should, with folded arms, only call on God for help, hasn't he reason to hope that the divine goodness will not refuse the favour of an extraordinary intervention to just and pure hands? These are dangerous examples, rare and sickly exceptions to our natural rules; we must yield to them, but with great moderation and caution. No private utility is so important that we should strain our consciences to that degree on its account; the public may be, when very plainly so and of very great moment.

Timoleon made a timely expiation for his strange exploit by the tears he shed, recalling that it was with a brother's hand he had killed the tyrant; and it justly pricked his conscience that he had been forced to buy public usefulness at so steep a price as the violation of his private morality. The Senate itself, which had been freed from slavery through him, did not dare give a clear verdict on so high a deed, and was divided between two equally important and opposed views of it. But the Syracusans, who at that same time were sending to the Corinthians to ask their protection and request a captain capable of restoring their city to its former dignity and ridding Sicily of the several petty tyrants who were oppressing it — the Corinthians deputed Timoleon for that service, with this clever declaration: "according as he should behave well or ill in his charge, their sentence would tend either to favour the deliverer of his country or to disfavour the murderer of his brother." This odd conclusion carries some excuse with it, by reason of the dangerous example and the importance of so strange an action; and they did well to take their own judgment out of it and refer it to others not so closely involved. But Timoleon's conduct in his expedition soon made his cause clearer, so worthily and virtuously did he comport himself on all occasions; and the good fortune that accompanied him in the difficulties he had to overcome in this noble employment seemed strewn in his way by the gods, who conspired favourably for his vindication.

The end of this story is excusable, if any can be; but the gain to the public treasury, which served the Roman Senate as a pretext for the foul conclusion I'm about to relate, is not enough to justify any such injustice.

Certain cities had bought back their freedom with money, by order and consent of the Senate, out of the hands of L. Sulla. The matter coming up again, the Senate condemned them to be taxable as they had been before, and ruled that the money they had paid for their redemption should be a dead loss to them. Civil war often produces such villainous examples: that we punish private men for trusting us back when we were public ministers, and the same magistrate makes another man pay the penalty for the magistrate's change of heart — when the man has no part in it. The schoolmaster whips his pupil for the pupil's docility; the guide beats the blind man he leads by the hand: a horrid image of justice.

There are rules in philosophy that are both false and feeble. The example proposed to us in favour of preferring private utility to a promise given doesn't carry weight enough, given the conditions they attach to it. Suppose robbers have seized you, and after making you swear to pay them a certain sum of money, set you free. It is not well to say that an honest man can be quit of his oath without paying, once he is out of their hands. Nothing of the kind: what fear once made me willing to do, I am bound to do when I am no longer afraid. And even if that fear had only prevailed on my tongue without forcing my will, I am still bound to keep my word. For my part, when my tongue has sometimes thoughtlessly said something I did not mean, I have made a point of conscience never to disown it. Otherwise, by degrees, we shall abolish all the right that another derives from our promises and oaths:
"Quasi vero forti viro vis possit adhiberi."
["As though a man of true courage could be forced." — Cicero, De Offic., iii. 30.]

And it is only lawful, on grounds of private interest, to excuse a breach of promise when we have promised something unlawful and wicked in itself; for the right of virtue must take precedence over the right of any obligation of ours.

I have placed Epaminondas before now in the first rank of excellent men, and I don't take it back. How far did he stretch the consideration of his own particular duty? He who never killed a man he had defeated; who, for the priceless benefit of restoring the liberty of his country, scrupled to kill a tyrant or his accomplices without due process of justice; and who reckoned anyone a wicked man, however good a citizen otherwise, who in battle among the enemy did not spare his friend and host. That was a soul of a rich composition: he married goodness and humanity — yes, the tenderest and most delicate kind in the whole school of philosophy — to the roughest and most violent of human actions. Was it nature or training that had so softened that great courage of his, so full, so obstinate against pain, death, and poverty, into such an extreme of sweetness and compassion? Dreadful in arms and blood, he overran and subdued a nation invincible by anyone else; and yet in the heat of an encounter, he could turn aside out of consideration for his friend and host. He was certainly fit to command in war who could so rein himself with the curb of good nature in the height and heat of his fury, a fury inflamed and foaming with blood and slaughter. It is a miracle to be able to mix any image of justice with such violent actions; and only such a steadiness of mind as Epaminondas's could blend with them sweetness and the ease of the gentlest manners and purest innocence. One man told the Mamertini that statutes were of no use against armed men; another told the people's tribune that the time of justice and the time of war were distinct things; a third said that the clash of arms drowned out the voice of the laws — but this man was not deaf to the laws of civility and pure courtesy. Had he not borrowed from his enemies the custom of sacrificing to the Muses when he went to war, so that their sweetness and gaiety might soften his martial and rigorous fury? Let us not fear, by the example of so great a master, to believe that there is something not lawful even against an enemy — and that the common cause should not demand everything from everyone against private interest:
"Manente memoria, etiam in dissidio publicorum foederum, privati juris:"
["The memory of private right remaining even amid public dissensions." — Livy, xxv. 18.]
"Et nulla potentia vires Praestandi, ne quid peccet amicus, habet;"
["No power on earth can sanction treachery against a friend." — Ovid, De Ponto, i. 7, 37.]
— and that not everything is lawful for an honest man in the service of his prince, the laws, or the general quarrel:
"Non enim patria praestat omnibus officiis.... et ipsi conducit pios habere cives in parentes."
["Duty to one's country does not override every other duty. The country itself benefits from having citizens who act piously toward their parents." — Cicero, De Offic., iii. 23.]

It is a lesson suited to the time we live in: we don't need to arm our courage with these weapons of steel; it's enough that our shoulders are accustomed to them. It's enough to dip our pens in ink without dipping them in blood. If it is grandeur of courage, and the effect of a rare and singular virtue, to despise friendship, private bonds, one's word and one's kin for the common good and obedience to the magistrate, it is certainly enough excuse for us that it is a grandeur which can have no place in the grandeur of Epaminondas's courage.
I detest those mad exhortations of that other troubled soul:
"Dum tela micant, non vos pietatis imago Ulla, nec adversa conspecti fronte parentes Commoveant; vultus gladio turbate verendos."
["While the swords flash, let no image of piety, not even the face of a father presented before you, move you: mar with your sword those venerable features." — Lucan, vii. 320.]

Let us deny to wicked, bloody, and treacherous natures any such pretext of reason; let us set aside this guilty and extravagant justice and stick to more human models. How much time and example can do! In a clash of the civil war against Cinna, one of Pompey's soldiers having unwittingly killed his own brother, who was on the other side, immediately killed himself out of shame and grief. Some years later, in another civil war among the same people, a soldier demanded a reward from his officer for having killed his brother.

A man poorly proves the honour and beauty of an action by its usefulness; and concludes very wrongly that everyone is obliged to do it, and that it suits everyone to do it, simply because it is useful:
"Omnia non pariter rerum sunt omnibus apta."
["All things are not equally fit for all men." — Propertius, iii. 9, 7.]

Take what is most necessary and useful for human society: it would be marriage. And yet the council of saints finds the contrary much better, excluding it from the most venerable calling of man — just as we set aside for stud the horses we think least of.

title: Of repentance
paragraphs: Others form man; I only report him: and I represent one particular man, ill made enough, whom, if I had to model anew, I should certainly make something other than what he is. But that's past recall. Now, though the features of my picture shift and change, it is not for that reason unlike: the world spins eternally; everything in it is incessantly in motion — the earth, the rocks of the Caucasus, the pyramids of Egypt — both by the general motion and by their own. Constancy itself is only a slower and more languishing motion. I cannot fix my object; it always staggers and reels with a natural giddiness; I take it as it is at the instant I consider it. I do not paint its being; I paint its passage — not the passage from one age to another, or, as the people say, from seven years to seven, but from day to day, from minute to minute. I must fit my history to the hour: I may change presently, not only by fortune but also by intention. It is a counterpart of various and changing accidents, of irresolute imaginations, and, as it falls out, sometimes contrary to one another: whether because I am then another self, or because I take up subjects under other circumstances and considerations. So it is that I may perhaps contradict myself; but, as Demades said, I never contradict the truth. If my soul could ever take footing, I would not be making essays — I would resolve; but it is always learning and trying itself out.

I propose a life ordinary and without lustre: it makes no difference; all moral philosophy may be applied as well to a common, private life as to one of richer composition. Every man bears the whole stamp of the human condition. Authors communicate themselves to the public by some particular external mark; I, the first of any, by my universal being — as Michel de Montaigne, not as a grammarian, a poet, or a lawyer. If the world finds fault that I speak too much of myself, I find fault that they don't even think about themselves. But is it reasonable that, while I'm so peculiar in my way of living, I should presume to recommend myself to the public's notice? And is it reasonable that I should present to the world — where art and polish carry such credit and authority — crude and simple effects of nature, and of a feeble nature at that? Isn't it building a wall without stones or bricks, or some such thing, to write books without learning and without art? The fancies of music are carried out by art; mine by chance. I have this much, at least, according to discipline: that no one ever treated of a subject he understood and knew better than I know what I have undertaken, and that in this I am the most understanding man alive. Secondly, no one ever went further into his matter, nor sifted its parts and consequences more closely and distinctly, nor more exactly and fully arrived at the goal he set himself. To bring it to completion, I need add nothing to the work but fidelity; and that's there, and the purest and most sincere kind to be found anywhere. I speak the truth — not as much as I would like to, but as much as I dare; and I dare a little more as I grow older, for, it seems to me, custom allows old age more liberty of prattle and more indiscretion in talking about oneself. What I often see elsewhere cannot happen here, where the work and the workman contradict one another: "Can a man of such sober conversation have written so foolish a book?" Or "Do such learned writings come from a man of such weak conversation?" Anyone who talks at a very ordinary rate and writes rare matter — it is to say his capacity is borrowed and not his own. A learned man is not learned in everything; but the sufficient man is sufficient throughout, even down to his ignorance: here my book and I go hand in hand together. Elsewhere people may praise or criticize the work without reference to the workman; here they cannot — whoever touches one touches the other. Anyone who judges of it without knowing him will wrong himself more than me; anyone who does know him gives me all the satisfaction I want. I shall be happier than I deserve if I can obtain only this much from public approval — to make men of understanding perceive that I was capable of profiting by knowledge, had I had it, and that I deserved to have been helped by a better memory.

Please excuse what I often repeat: that I very rarely repent, and that my conscience is content with itself — not as the conscience of an angel, or that of a horse, but as the conscience of a man; always adding this qualification, not as a courtesy but a true and real submission, that I speak in inquiry and doubt, referring myself purely and simply to the common and accepted beliefs for the resolution. I do not teach; I only relate.

There is no vice that is absolutely a vice that does not give offence, and that a sound judgment does not condemn; for there is so manifest a deformity and inconvenience in it that perhaps those are right who say it is chiefly bred by stupidity and ignorance — so hard is it to imagine that anyone can know a vice without hating it. Malice sucks up most of its own venom and poisons itself. Vice leaves repentance in the soul like an ulcer in the flesh, always scratching and lacerating itself; for reason effaces every other grief and sorrow, but it gives birth to that of repentance, which is so much the more painful in that it springs from within — just as the heat and cold of fevers are sharper than those that only touch the outer skin. I count as vices (each according to its proportion) not only those that reason and nature condemn, but also those that the opinion of men — though false and mistaken — has made such, when they are sanctioned by law and custom.

And there is no virtue, equally, that does not give pleasure to a well-bred nature: there is a kind of, I don't know what, self-congratulation in doing well that gives us an inward satisfaction, and a generous boldness that goes with a good conscience. A daringly vicious soul may, perhaps, arm itself with confidence, but it cannot supply itself with this contentment and satisfaction. It is no small satisfaction to feel oneself preserved from the contagion of so corrupt an age, and to be able to say to oneself: "Whoever could penetrate into my soul would not find me guilty there, either of the affliction or ruin of anyone, or of revenge or envy, or of any offence against the public laws, or of innovation or disturbance, or breach of my word; and though the licence of the times permits and even teaches everyone to do otherwise, yet I have never plundered any Frenchman's goods or taken his money, and have lived on what is my own, in war as in peace; nor have I set any man to work without paying him his hire." These testimonies of a good conscience are pleasant, and this natural rejoicing is very beneficial to us, and the only reward we can never fail of.

To base the recompense of virtuous actions on the approval of others is too uncertain and unsafe a foundation — especially in so corrupt and ignorant an age as this, in which the good opinion of the crowd is an insult. On whom can you rely to show you what deserves commendation? God forbid I should be an honest man according to the descriptions of honour I see everyone daily make of himself:
"Quae fuerant vitia, mores sunt."
["What used to be vices are now manners." — Seneca, Ep., 39.]

Some of my friends have at times taken me to task and scolded me with great sincerity and plainness, either of their own initiative or at my asking — for to a well-composed soul, that is an office which surpasses, not only in usefulness but in kindness, all other offices of friendship. I have always received their corrections with the most open arms, both of courtesy and gratitude; but to tell the truth, I have often found so much false measure both in their reproaches and their praises that I would not have done much amiss to have done badly rather than well according to their notions. Those of us who live private lives, exposed to no other gaze than our own, ought above all to have a model settled within ourselves by which to test our actions; and according to that, sometimes to encourage ourselves and sometimes to correct ourselves. I have my own laws and my own court to judge myself by, and I apply myself more to these than to any other rules. I do, indeed, restrain my actions by the standards of others; but I extend them only by my own. Only you know whether you are cowardly and cruel, loyal and devout: others do not see you, and only guess at you by uncertain conjectures; they see your art rather than your nature. So don't rely on their opinions; stick to your own:
"Tuo tibi judicio est utendum.... Virtutis et vitiorum grave ipsius conscientiae pondus est: qua sublata, jacent omnia."

["You must use your own judgment upon yourself; great is the weight of your own conscience in the discovery of virtues and vices; if that is taken away, everything collapses." — Cicero, De Nat. Dei, iii. 35; Tusc. Quaes., i. 25.]

But the saying that repentance follows hard on the heels of sin doesn't seem to refer to sin in its full estate, lodged in us as in its own dwelling. We may disown and renounce the vices that take us by surprise, the ones we are swept into by our passions; but those that have rooted themselves in a strong and vigorous will by long habit cannot be contradicted. Repentance is nothing but a recanting of the will and an opposition to our fancies, which lead us wherever they please. It makes this man disown his former virtue and self-control:
"Quae mens est hodie, cur eadem non puero fait? Vel cur his animis incolumes non redeunt genae?"
["Why was not the mind I have today the same when I was a boy? Or why do my cheeks not return unspoiled to the feelings I had then?" — Horace, Od., iv. 10, 7.]

It is a precise life that keeps itself in good order in private. Anyone can play a part and look like an honest man on the stage; but within, in his own bosom, where everyone may do as he likes and where everything is hidden — to be regular there, that's the point. The next degree is to be regular in his house, in his daily actions, for which we are accountable to no one and where there is no study or artifice. So Bias, setting forth the excellent state of a private family, says: "such a one as the master is within, by his own virtue and temper, that he is abroad, for fear of the laws and people's reports." And it was a worthy saying of Julius Drusus, to the masons who offered him, for three thousand crowns, to fix his house so that his neighbours could no longer have the same view into it as before: "I will give you," he said, "six thousand to make it so that everybody can see into every room." It is recorded as honourable of Agesilaus that on his journeys he always took up his lodgings in temples, so that the people and the gods themselves could pry into his most private actions. Some men have been a wonder to the world in whom neither wife nor servant ever saw anything remarkable; few men have been admired by their own household; no one was ever a prophet, not just in his own house, but in his own country either — so the experience of histories tells us. It is the same in trifling things; even in this low example one may see the image of a greater one. In my country of Gascony they consider it a curiosity to see me in print: the further from home I am read, the better I am thought of. I have to pay printers in Guienne; elsewhere they pay me. It is on this principle that those build who hide themselves while present and living, in order to gain a name when they are dead and absent. I would rather have a great deal less in hand; I expose myself to the world on no other account than my present share, and when I leave the world I quit the rest. See this functionary whom the people escort in state, with awe and applause, right to his door; he sheds the pageant with his robe, and falls so much the lower the higher he had been exalted: within himself, all is in tumult and disorder. And even if all were well-ordered there, it will take a lively and well-chosen judgment to detect it in these low and private actions; to which one may add that order is a dull, sombre virtue. To storm a breach, conduct an embassy, govern a people — these are actions of renown; to scold, laugh, sell, pay, love, hate, and gently and justly converse with one's own family and with oneself; not to relax, not to give oneself the lie — these are rarer and harder, and less noticed. By which means, retired lives, whatever may be said to the contrary, perform duties as great as or greater than the others; and private men, says Aristotle, serve virtue more painfully and worthily than men in office. We prepare ourselves for grand occasions more out of vanity than conscience. The shortest way to glory would be to do for conscience what we do for glory. Alexander's virtue strikes me as having much less vigour on his great stage than that of Socrates in his low and obscure employment. I can easily imagine Socrates in Alexander's place; but Alexander in Socrates' — I cannot. Ask the one what he can do, he will answer, "Subdue the world"; ask the other the same question, he will say, "Live human life according to its natural condition" — a much more general, weighty, and legitimate science than the other.

The virtue of the soul does not consist in flying high but in walking orderly; its grandeur is exercised not in greatness, but in moderation. Just as those who judge and try us within make no great account of the brilliance of our public actions, and see that they are only streaks and rays of clear water springing from a muddy bottom, so too those who judge us by our gallant outward show conclude the same about our inner constitution, and cannot pair the common faculties they have with the others that astonish them, and which are so far out of their sight. This is why we give such savage forms to demons; and who does not give Tamerlane great eyebrows, wide nostrils, a frightful face, and a prodigious stature, according to the picture his name calls up? Had anyone brought me to Erasmus some time ago, I would hardly have believed but that everything he said to his man or his hostess was adage and apothegm. We much more easily picture a craftsman on his close-stool, or with his wife, than a great judge venerable by his bearing and competence: we imagine that, from their lofty tribunals, they will not stoop so far as to live. As vicious souls are often spurred by some outside impulse to do well, so are virtuous souls to do ill; they are therefore to be judged by their settled state, when they are at home, whenever that may be; and at any rate when they are closest to repose and in their native station.

Natural inclinations are greatly assisted and reinforced by education; but they seldom alter and overcome their original make-up. A thousand natures of my time have escaped toward virtue or toward vice, against a quite contrary discipline:

"Sic ubi, desuetae silvis, in carcere clausae Mansuevere ferx, et vultus posuere minaces, Atque hominem didicere pati, si torrida parvus Venit in ora cruor, redeunt rabiesque fororque, Admonitaeque tument gustato sanguine fauces Fervet, et a trepido vix abstinet ira magistro;"

["So savage beasts, when shut up in cages and grown unaccustomed to the woods, become tame, lay aside their fierce looks, and submit to man's rule; but if even a small taste of warm blood comes into their mouths, their rage and fury return, their jaws swell at the taste of blood, and their anger scarcely abstains from their trembling master." — Lucan, iv. 237.]

— these original qualities are not to be rooted out; they may be covered and concealed. The Latin tongue is in a sense natural to me; I understand it better than French; but I have not been used to speaking it, or hardly even to writing it, for forty years. And yet, under extreme and sudden emotions, of which I have had two or three in my life — once when I saw my father in perfect health collapse on me in a faint — I have always uttered my first words from the bottom of my heart in Latin, nature breaking through and forcing itself out in spite of so long a disuse. And the same thing is reported of many others.

Those who have tried in my time to correct men's manners by new opinions reform apparent vices; the essential vices they leave as they were, when they don't actually enlarge them — and that enlargement is what we have to fear. We postpone all other doing of good on the strength of these external reforms, which cost less and look more impressive, and so we expiate cheaply for our other natural, consubstantial, and inward vices. Look a little into our experience: there is no one who, if he listens to himself, doesn't discover within himself a particular and dominant form of his own that wrestles with his education and with the storm of passions that run against it. For my part, I am rarely much shaken by surprises; I always find myself in my place, as heavy and unwieldy bodies do. If I am not at home, I am always near it; my wanderings don't carry me very far; nothing strange or extreme happens; and yet I do have sound and vigorous turns.

The real condemnation, which touches the common practice of men, is that even their solitary retirement is full of filth and corruption; the idea of their reformation muddled, their repentance ailing and faulty almost as much as their sin. Some, either from having been bound to vice by a natural bent or by long habit, can no longer see its deformity. Others (and I am of this constitution) feel the weight of vice, but counterbalance it with pleasure or some other compensation; they put up with it and lend themselves to it for a certain price — but viciously and basely. One could perhaps imagine so vast a disproportion of measure that the pleasure might justly excuse the sin, as we say happens with utility — not only when the pleasure is accidental and outside the sin, as in theft, but in the very act of sinning, or in the enjoyment of women, where the temptation is violent and, it is said, sometimes not to be overcome.

Being the other day in Armagnac, on the estate of a relative of mine, I saw a peasant whom everyone nicknamed "the thief". This is how he told the story of his life: that being born a beggar, and finding that he would not be able, by the sweat of his brow, to free himself from poverty, he resolved to become a thief, and by means of his bodily strength had practised this trade all through his youth in great safety. For he always made his harvest and his vintage in other men's grounds — but a great way off, and in such quantities that it seemed unbelievable that one man could carry away so much on his shoulders in one night. Furthermore, he was careful to spread out and divide the damage so that the loss was of less importance to any one man in particular. He is now grown old, and rich for a man of his station, thanks to his trade, which he openly confesses to everyone. And to make his peace with God, he says he is daily ready by good offices to make restitution to the heirs of those he has robbed; and if he doesn't finish (which he can't do all at once), he will leave the rest in charge to his heirs, in proportion to the wrong he, and only he, knows he has done each one. By this account, true or false, the man looks on theft as a dishonest action and hates it, but less than he hates poverty, and so simply repents; but to the extent he has thus made restitution, he does not repent. This is not the habit which incorporates us into vice and conforms even our understanding to it; nor is it the impetuous whirlwind that troubles and blinds our soul by gusts and, for the time, hurries us, judgment and all, into the power of vice.

I customarily do thoroughly whatever I do, and take but one step on it; I rarely have any movement that hides itself or steals away from my reason, and that doesn't proceed in the matter by the consent of all my faculties, without division or internal sedition. My judgment gets all the blame or all the praise; and the blame, once it has, it keeps; for from my infancy on, it has always been one and the same — the same inclination, the same turn, the same force. And as for general convictions, I fixed myself from childhood in the place where I resolved to stay. There are sins that are impetuous, prompt, and sudden — let us set them aside. But in these other sins, so often repeated, deliberated, contrived — whether sins of complexion or of profession and vocation — I cannot conceive that they should have lodged themselves so long in the same resolution unless the reason and conscience of the man who has them is steady in wanting to have them; and the repentance he claims is inspired in him on a sudden is very hard for me to imagine or shape. I don't follow the opinion of the Pythagorean sect, "that men take up a new soul when they go to the images of the gods to receive their oracles" — unless they mean that it must indeed be extrinsic, new, and lent for the time; our own showing so little sign of purification and cleanness fit for such an office.

They act quite contrary to the Stoic precepts, who command us to correct the imperfections and vices we are aware of in ourselves but forbid us to disturb the repose of our soul on their account: these people make us believe they have great grief and remorse within them, but they show nothing of amendment, correction, or interruption. It cannot be a cure if the malady isn't entirely discharged; if repentance were placed on the scale of the balance, it would outweigh sin. I know no quality so easy to counterfeit as devotion, if men do not conform their behaviour and life to the profession; its essence is hidden and obscure, the appearance easy and showy.

For my own part, I may desire in general to be other than I am; I may condemn and dislike my whole form, and beg of Almighty God for an entire reformation, and pray that he will please to pardon my natural infirmity. But I ought not to call this repentance, it seems to me, any more than my dissatisfaction at not being an angel or Cato. My actions are regular and conformable to what I am and to my condition; I can do no better; and repentance does not properly touch things that are not in our power — sorrow does. I imagine an infinite number of natures more elevated and well-ordered than mine; and yet I do not for that reason improve my faculties, any more than my arm or will grow stronger and more vigorous from my conceiving someone else's to be so. If our conceiving and wishing for a nobler way of acting than ours should produce repentance for our own way, we should have to repent of our most innocent actions, since we may well suppose that in a more excellent nature they would have been carried out with greater dignity and perfection — and we wish that ours had been so. When I look back on the conduct of my youth and compare it with my old age, I find that I have generally behaved with equal regularity in both, according to my understanding: that is all my resistance can do. I do not flatter myself: in the same circumstances I should do the same things again. It is not a patch but rather a universal tincture with which I am stained. I know no repentance that is superficial, half-hearted, ceremonial; it must sting me all over before I can call it that, and must prick my bowels as deeply and as universally as God sees into me.

As for business, many excellent opportunities have escaped me for want of good management; and yet my decisions were sound enough, given what was before me — they tend always to choose the easiest and safest course. I find that in my past resolves I have proceeded with discretion, according to my own rule and according to the state of the subject proposed; and I should do the same a thousand years from now in like cases. I am not considering what the matter is now, but what it was then, when I was deliberating on it: all the force of advice consists in the time; the occasions and the things shift and change continually. In my life I have made some important mistakes, not for want of good understanding but for want of good luck. There are secret, unforeseen parts in the matters we have in hand — especially in the nature of men — silent conditions that make no show, unknown sometimes even to those who possess them, that spring up and start on the occasion. If my prudence could not penetrate them or foresee them, I do not blame it: it has its commission only within its limits. If the event proves too hard for me, and takes the side I refused, there is no help for it; I do not blame myself, I accuse my fortune and not my work. That cannot be called repentance.

Phocion, having given the Athenians an advice that was not followed, and the affair turning out contrary to his opinion, someone said to him, "Well, Phocion, are you happy that things have gone so well?" — "I am very happy," he replied, "that this has happened so well, but I do not repent giving the other advice." When friends of mine come to me for advice, I give it candidly and clearly, without sticking — as nearly everyone else does — at the risk that the thing might turn out contrary to my opinion and that I might be reproached for my counsel. I am quite indifferent on that score; the fault will be theirs for having consulted me, and I could not refuse them that office.

I, for my own part, can rarely blame anyone but myself for my mistakes and misfortunes; for in truth I seldom ask the advice of another, except by way of polite ceremony, or where I need information, special expertise, or facts. But in things where I need only judgment, the reasons of others may serve to back up my own, but have little power to dissuade me from it; I hear them all with civility and patience, but to my recollection, I have never used any but my own. To me, others' reasons are only flies and atoms, confusing and distracting my will. I lay no great weight on my own opinions; but I lay just as little on those of others, and fortune rewards me accordingly: if I get little advice, I give little too. I am seldom consulted, and even more seldom believed, and I know no business, public or private, that has been mended or bettered by my advice. Even those whom fortune had in some way put under my direction have more willingly let themselves be governed by other counsels than mine. And as a man who is as jealous of my repose as of my authority, I am better pleased that it should be so; in leaving me there, they fall in with what I profess, which is to settle and contain myself wholly within myself. I take pleasure in being uninterested in other men's affairs, and disengaged from being their guarantor and responsible for what they do.

In all affairs that are past, however they turned out, I have very little regret; for this consideration sets me at ease — that they were bound to fall out as they did, in the great revolution of the world, and in the chain of Stoic causes. Your fancy cannot, by wish and imagination, move a single tittle without the great current of things reversing both the past and the future.

As for the rest, I detest that incidental repentance which old age brings with it. The man who said long ago that he was obliged to age for having weaned him from pleasure was of a different mind than I am; I will never think myself indebted to impotence for any good it may do me:
"Nec tam aversa unquam videbitur ab opere suo providentia, ut debilitas inter optima inventa sit."
["Nor can Providence ever seem so averse to her own work that debility should be reckoned among the best of things." — Quintilian, Instit. Orat., v. 12.]

Our appetites are rare in old age; a profound satiety seizes us after the act: in this I see nothing of conscience; chagrin and weakness imprint in us a drowsy and rheumatic virtue. We must not let ourselves be so wholly carried away by natural changes that we let our judgments be imposed on by them. Youth and pleasure did not formerly so far prevail with me that I could not still discern the face of vice in pleasure; nor does the distaste years have brought me now so prevail with me that I cannot discern pleasure in vice. Now that I am no longer in my flourishing age, I judge of these things as well as if I were.
["Old though I am, for ladies' love unfit, / The power of beauty I remember yet." — Chaucer.]

I, who examine it narrowly and strictly, find my reason just the same as it was in my most licentious age — except, perhaps, that it is weaker and more decayed by being grown older. And I find that the pleasure it refuses me on account of my bodily health, it would no more refuse me now, on account of the health of my soul, than at any time before. I do not reckon it the more valiant for not being able to combat; my temptations are so broken and mortified that they are not worth its opposition; holding out my hands, I repel them. Were one to set the old concupiscence before it, I fear it would have less power to resist than before. I cannot see that in itself it now judges anything otherwise than it did before, or that it has gained any new light. Therefore, if there is any convalescence in me, it is an enchanted one. Miserable kind of remedy, to owe one's health to one's disease! It is not for our misfortune to perform this office, but for the good fortune of our judgment. Persecutions and afflictions are not what move me — they make me curse them: that is for people who can only be roused with a whip. My reason is much freer in prosperity, and much more distracted and put to it to digest pains than pleasures. I see best in a clear sky; health admonishes me more cheerfully and to better purpose than sickness. I did all that lay in me to reform and regulate myself away from pleasures at a time when I had health and vigour to enjoy them; I should be ashamed and envious if the misery and misfortune of my old age were to have credit over my good, healthy, sprightly, and vigorous years, and that men should estimate me not by what I have been but by what I have ceased to be.

In my opinion, it is happy living, not (as Antisthenes said) happy dying, that human felicity consists in. I have not made it my business to fix the monstrous addition of a philosopher's tail onto the head and body of a libertine; nor do I want this wretched remainder to give the lie to the pleasant, sound, and long part of my life: I would present myself uniformly throughout. If I were to live my life over again, I should live it just as I have lived it; I neither complain of the past nor fear the future; and if I am not much deceived, I am the same within as I am without. It is one main obligation I owe to my fortune, that the succession of my bodily estate has gone according to the natural seasons; I have seen the grass, the blossom, the fruit, and now I see the withering — happily, however, because naturally. I bear the infirmities I have the better, because they didn't come till I had reason to expect them, and also because they make me remember with greater pleasure the long happiness of my past life. My wisdom may have been just the same in both ages, but it was more active and of better grace while young and lively than now, when it is broken, peevish, and uneasy. So I reject these casual and painful reformations. God must touch our hearts; our consciences must amend of themselves by the help of our reason, not by the decay of our appetites; pleasure is not in itself pale or discoloured, only to be discerned by dim and decayed eyes.

We ought to love temperance for its own sake, and because God has commanded it and chastity; but what we are reduced to by catarrhs, and what I owe to the stone, is neither chastity nor temperance. A man cannot boast he despises and resists pleasure if he cannot see it, if he doesn't know what it is, if he cannot make out its graces, its force, and its most alluring beauties. I know both the one and the other, and may therefore the better say so. But it seems to me that our souls in old age are subject to more troublesome maladies and imperfections than in youth; I said the same when I was young and was reproached for having no beard, and I say it now that my grey hairs give me some authority. We call the difficulty of our humours and our distaste for present things wisdom; but in truth we do not so much forsake our vices as exchange them — and, in my opinion, for worse. Besides a foolish and feeble pride, an impertinent prating, surly and unsociable humours, superstition, and a ridiculous desire for riches when we have lost the use of them, I find there more envy, injustice, and malice. Age leaves more wrinkles in the mind than it does on the face; and souls are never, or very rarely, seen that in growing old do not smell sour and musty. Man moves all together, both toward his perfection and his decay. Observing the wisdom of Socrates and several circumstances of his condemnation, I dare to believe that he in some way deliberately, by collusion, contributed to it, since at the age of seventy he might fear to see the lofty motions of his mind cramped and his accustomed lustre obscured. What strange metamorphoses do I see age make every day in many of my acquaintances! It is a potent malady, and one that naturally and imperceptibly steals into us; a great deal of study and great precaution are needed to avoid the imperfections it loads us with, or at least to slow their progress. I find that, in spite of all my entrenchments, it gets foot by foot upon me; I resist as best I can, but I do not know what at last it will reduce me to. But come what may, I am content for the world to know, when I have fallen, from what I fell.

title: Of three commerces
paragraphs: We must not rivet ourselves so fast to our humours and temperaments: our chief ability is to know how to apply ourselves to different employments. It is to be, but not to live, to keep oneself tied and bound by necessity to a single course; the bravest souls are those that have in them the most variety and pliancy. Here is an honourable testimony of the elder Cato:
"Huic versatile ingenium sic pariter ad omnia fuit, ut natum ad id unum diceres, quodcumque ageret."
["His gifts were so pliable to every use that you would have said he had been born only for whatever he happened to be doing." — Livy, xxxix. 49.]

If I had the liberty to fashion myself in my own mode, there is no manner so graceful that I would so fix myself to it as not to be able to disengage from it. Life is an unequal, irregular, and multiform motion. It is not to be a friend to oneself, much less a master, but a slave, to be incessantly led by the nose by one's self, and to be so fixed in one's previous inclinations that one cannot turn aside or wrench one's neck out of the collar. I say this now in this part of my life when I find I cannot easily disengage myself from the importunity of my own soul, which cannot ordinarily occupy itself but in things of limited range, nor employ itself except entirely and with all its force. On the lightest subject thrown to it, it expands and stretches itself to that degree that it employs its utmost powers on it; so that idleness is a very painful labour to me, and very damaging to my health. Most men's minds need foreign matter to exercise and enliven them; mine has rather a need of it to sit still and rest:
"Vitia otii negotio discutienda sunt,"
["The vices of idleness must be shaken off by business." — Seneca, Ep. 56.]

— for its chief and hardest study is to study itself. Books are a sort of employment for it that draws it away from that study. With the first thoughts that take possession of it, it begins to bustle and test its vigour in every direction, exercising its powers of handling — now testing its strength, now fortifying, moderating, and arranging itself by way of grace and order. It has of its own enough to rouse its faculties: nature has given it, as it has given everyone else, matter enough of its own to take advantage of, and subjects fit enough on which it may either invent or judge.

Meditation is a strong and full study for those who can effectively taste it and apply themselves to it; I would rather shape my soul than furnish it. There is no employment, either feebler or stronger, than that of entertaining one's own thoughts, depending on what kind of soul one has; the greatest men make it their whole business,
"Quibus vivere est cogitare;"
["For whom to live is to think." — Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., v. 28.]

— nature has therefore favoured it with this privilege, that there is nothing we can do for so long, nor any action we more often and easily give ourselves up to. It is the business of the gods, says Aristotle, and the source of both their beatitude and ours.

The main use of reading, for me, is that by its various objects it rouses my reason and exercises my judgment — not my memory. Few conversations hold me without effort and strain. It is true that beauty and elegance of speech take with me as much as, or more than, the weight and depth of the subject; and since I am apt to be sleepy in all other kinds of talk and give only the rind of my attention, it often happens that in such poor and pitiful conversations — mere chatter — I either make drowsy, unmeaning answers, unbecoming a child and ridiculous, or, more foolishly and rudely still, keep an obstinate silence. I have a pensive way that withdraws me into myself; and along with that, a heavy and childish ignorance of many very ordinary things — by which two qualities I have earned this, that people can truly tell five or six tales as ridiculous about me as about any other man whatever.

But, to proceed with my subject, this difficult constitution of mine makes me very particular about the company I keep with men: I must select and pick them out for my purpose; and it unfits me for common society. We live and have to deal with the public; if their conversation is troublesome to us, if we disdain to apply ourselves to ordinary and vulgar souls (and the ordinary and vulgar are often as regular as those of the finest thread, and all wisdom is folly that does not accommodate itself to the common ignorance), we must give up meddling either with other people's affairs or our own; for business, both public and private, has to do with such people. The least forced and most natural motions of the soul are the finest; the best employments are those least strained. My God, what a good office wisdom does those whose desires it limits to their power! That is the most useful knowledge: "according to what a man can," was Socrates' favourite saying and motto. A motto of great solidity.

We must moderate and adapt our desires to the nearest and easiest things to obtain. Is it not a foolish whim of mine to separate myself from a thousand people to whom my fortune has joined me, and without whom I cannot live, and cleave to one or two who are outside my circle — or rather a fantastic desire for something I cannot obtain? My gentle and easy manners, enemies of all sourness and harshness, may easily enough have saved me from being envied or hated; to be loved, I won't say, but no man ever gave less occasion to be hated. Yet the coldness of my conversation has, reasonably enough, deprived me of the goodwill of many, who may be excused if they interpret it in another and worse sense.

I am very capable of contracting and maintaining rare and exquisite friendships; for since I so greedily seize on the acquaintances that suit my liking, I throw myself with such violence on them that I hardly fail to stick fast and to leave an impression wherever I hit — as I have often happily proven. In ordinary friendships I am somewhat cold and shy, because my motion is not natural when not under full sail. Besides, my fortune having in my youth given me a taste for one sole and perfect friendship, has, in truth, made others somewhat distasteful to me, and stamped too deeply on my mind that friendship is a beast of company, as the ancient said, but not of the herd. I also have a natural difficulty in communicating myself by halves, with the qualifications and the servile, jealous prudence required in the company of numerous and imperfect friendships — and we are mostly thrust onto these in this age of ours, when we cannot talk about the world except either with danger or in falsehood.

Yet I see clearly enough that anyone who has the conveniences of life (I mean the essential conveniences) for his end, as I do, should avoid these difficulties and this delicacy of humour as much as the plague. I would praise a soul of several storeys, that knows both how to stretch itself and to slacken — that finds itself at ease in every condition fortune leads it into; that can talk with a neighbour about his building, his hunting, his quarrels; that can chat with a carpenter or a gardener with pleasure. I envy those who can render themselves familiar with the meanest of their followers and talk with them in their own way; and I dislike Plato's advice, that men should always speak in a magisterial tone to their servants, men or women, without sometimes being playful and familiar; for besides the reasons I have given, it is inhumane and unjust to put such great value on this pitiful prerogative of fortune. The polities where less disparity is permitted between masters and servants seem to me the most equitable. Others study how to raise and elevate their minds; I, how to humble mine and to bring it low; it is only vicious in its expansion:
"Narras et genus AEaci, Et pugnata sacro bella sub Ilio Quo Chium pretio cadum Mercemur, quis aquam temperet ignibus, Quo praebente domum, et quota, Pelignis caream frigoribus, taces."

["You tell us long tales about the race of Aeacus, and the battles fought under sacred Ilium; but what to give for a cask of Chian wine, who will prepare the warm bath, in whose house, and when I may escape the Pelignian cold — that you do not tell us." — Horace, Od., iii. 19, 3.]

Thus, as the Lacedaemonian valour needed moderation, and the sweet and harmonious sound of flutes to soften it in battle, lest they should rush themselves into rashness and fury — whereas other nations commonly use harsh and shrill sounds, and loud and imperious cries, to incite and heat the soldier's courage to the last degree — so too, in my opinion, contrary to the usual method, in the conduct of our minds we have for the most part more need of lead than of wings, of temperance and composure than of ardour and agitation. But, above all, I think it egregiously foolish to put on the grave airs of a man of lofty mind among those who are nothing of the sort: forever to speak in print (as if by the book),
"Favellare in puma di forchetta."
["To talk with the point of a fork," i.e. affectedly.]

You must let yourself down to those you converse with, and sometimes affect ignorance; lay aside power and subtlety in common talk; to preserve decorum and order, that is enough — nay, crawl on the earth, if they so wish.

The learned often stumble at this stone; they will always be parading their pedantic science and strewing their books everywhere; in our day they have so filled the cabinets and the ears of ladies with them that if the ladies have lost the substance, they at least retain the words; so that in any kind of talk, on whatever subject, however mean and common, they speak and write in a new and learned way,
"Hoc sermone pavent, hoc iram, gaudia, curas, Hoc cuncta effundunt animi secreta; quid ultra? Concumbunt docte;"

["In this language they express their fears, their anger, their joys, their cares; in this they pour out all the secrets of their souls; what more? They lie with their lovers learnedly." — Juvenal, vi. 189.]

— and quote Plato and Aquinas on matters the first man they meet could settle as well. The learning that cannot penetrate their souls hangs still upon the tongue. If people of quality would be persuaded by me, they should be content to set out their own proper and natural treasures: they conceal and cover their beauties under others that are not theirs. It is great folly to put out one's own light and shine by a borrowed lustre; they are buried under "de capsula totae" — completely out of their box. It is because they don't sufficiently know themselves or do themselves justice: the world has nothing fairer than them; it's for them to honour the arts and to paint painting itself. What need have they of anything but to live loved and honoured? They have and know but too much for that purpose: they need only rouse and warm a little the faculties they have of their own. When I see them tampering with rhetoric, law, logic, and other such drugs — so improper and unnecessary for their business — I begin to suspect that the men who fill them with such notions do it that they may govern them on that account; for what other excuse can I find? It is enough that, without our instruction, they can compose the graces of their eyes for gaiety, gravity, or sweetness, and season a refusal with sharpness, suspense, or favour; they need no one else to interpret what we say in their service. With this knowledge, they command with a switch, and rule both the tutors and the schools. But if, nevertheless, it angers them to give place to us in anything whatever, and they will out of curiosity have their share in books, poetry is a diversion proper for them: a wanton, subtle, dissembling, prating art, all pleasure and all show, like themselves. They may also extract several commodities from history. From philosophy, out of its moral part, they may select such instructions as will teach them to judge of our humours and conditions, to defend themselves from our treacheries, to regulate the ardour of their own desires, to manage their liberty, to lengthen the pleasures of life, and gently to bear the inconstancy of a lover, the rudeness of a husband, the encroachment of years and wrinkles, and the like. This is the utmost I would allow them in the sciences.

There are some particular natures that are private and retired; my natural way is suited to communication and apt to lay me open. I am all without and in sight, born for society and friendship. The solitude that I love myself and recommend to others is chiefly nothing other than to withdraw my thoughts and affections into myself: to restrain and check, not my steps, but my own cares and desires; resigning all foreign solicitude, and avoiding to death servitude and obligation, and not so much the crowd of men as the crowd of business. Local solitude, to tell the truth, rather gives me more room and sets me more at large; I more readily throw myself onto affairs of state and of the world when I am alone. At the Louvre and in the bustle of the court, I fold myself within my own skin; the crowd pushes me back onto myself; and I never entertain myself so wantonly, with so much licence, or so particularly, as in places of respect and ceremonious caution. Our follies do not make me laugh; it is our wisdom that does. I am not by nature an enemy of court life; I have spent part of mine there, and am of a temperament cheerfully to frequent great company, provided it be at intervals and at my own time. But this delicacy of judgment I'm speaking of perforce ties me to solitude. Even at home, amid a numerous family and in a house frequently visited, I see people enough, but rarely such as I delight to converse with; and I there reserve, both for myself and others, an unusual liberty: there is in my house no such thing as ceremony, ushering, or seeing people down to the coach, and other such troublesome ceremonies as our politeness enjoins (O servile and importunate custom!). Everyone there governs himself by his own method; let whoever wishes speak his thoughts; I sit mute, meditating and shut up in my closet, without any offence to my guests.

The men whose society and familiarity I covet are those they call sincere and able men; and the image of these makes me disrelish the rest. It is, rightly understood, the rarest of our forms, and a form we chiefly owe to nature. The end of this commerce is simply intimacy, frequenting and conferring, the exercise of souls, without any other fruit. In our conversations, all subjects are alike to me; whether there is weight or depth or not, it is all one; there is always grace and pertinency; everything in them is tinted with a mature and constant judgment, and mixed with goodness, freedom, gaiety, and friendship. It is not only in talking of the affairs of kings and state that our wits show their force and beauty, but every bit as much in private conferences. I know my men by their silences and their smiles, and discover them better, perhaps, at table than in council. Hippomachus said very well that he could tell good wrestlers just by seeing them walk in the street. If learning chooses to step into our talk, it shall not be rejected — not magisterial, imperious, and obtrusive, as it commonly is, but subordinate and docile itself: we are there only to pass the time. When we want to be instructed and preached at, we will go look for that on its throne; let it humble itself to us for the moment. For useful and profitable as it is, I imagine we can, when need be, manage well enough without it, and do our business without its help. A well-born soul, practised in the conversation of men, will of herself render herself sufficiently agreeable; art is nothing but the counterpart and register of what such souls produce.
The conversation of beautiful and honourable women is also a sweet commerce to me:
"Nam nos quoque oculos eruditos habemus."
["For we too have eyes that are versed in the matter." — Cicero, Paradox, v. 2.]

If the soul has not so much to enjoy in this commerce as in the first, the bodily senses, which participate more here, bring it to a level next to it — though, in my opinion, not equal to it. But it is a commerce in which one must stand a little on his guard, especially someone like me in whom the body can do much. I scalded myself in my youth at it, and suffered all the torments that poets say befall those who fling themselves into love without order and judgment. It is true that that whipping has made me wiser since:
"Quicumque Argolica de classe Capharea fugit, Semper ab Euboicis vela retorquet aquis."
["Whoever of the Greek fleet escaped the Caphareus rocks ever takes care to steer clear of the Euboean sea." — Ovid, Trist., i. 1, 83.]

It is folly to fix all one's thoughts upon it and engage in it with a furious and indiscreet affection; but on the other hand, to engage there without love and without inclination, like an actor, to play a common part, putting in nothing of one's own but words, is to provide for one's safety, but in as cowardly a way as one who would abandon his honour, profit, or pleasure for fear of danger. For it is certain that from such a practice, those who set it on foot can expect no fruit that can please or satisfy a noble soul.
