In another place, the young men publicly cut through, between the skin and the flesh of that part, in several places, and pushed pieces of wood into the openings as long and thick as they would receive, and afterwards made a fire of those pieces of wood as an offering to their gods; they were reckoned neither vigorous nor chaste if by the force of that cruel pain they showed any dismay. Elsewhere the most sacred magistrate was reverenced and acknowledged by that member, and in various ceremonies an effigy of it was carried in procession in honour of various deities. The Egyptian ladies, in their Bacchanalia, each carried one finely carved of wood about their necks, as large and heavy as she could so carry; besides which, the statue of their god presented one which surpassed all the rest of his body in size. The married women in the region where I live make of their kerchiefs the figure of one upon their foreheads, to glorify themselves in their enjoyment of it, and on becoming widows they throw it behind and cover it with their head-cloths. The most modest matrons of Rome thought it an honour to offer flowers and garlands to the god Priapus, and they made the virgins, at the time of their espousals, sit upon his shameful parts. And I am not sure I have not in my own time seen some air of similar devotion. What was the meaning of that ridiculous bit of our forefathers' clothing — and still worn by our Swiss? Why do we make a show of our equipment in figure under our breeches, and often, even worse, above its natural size, by falsehood and imposture? I have half a mind to believe that this sort of garment was invented in those better, more conscientious ages, that the world might not be deceived, and that every man should give a public account of his proportions. The simple peoples wear them still, and around their real size. Back then, the tailor took measure of it as the shoemaker now does of a man's foot. That worthy man who, when I was young, gelded so many noble and ancient statues in his great city, so they should not corrupt the eyesight of the ladies — following the advice of this other ancient worthy:
"Flagitii principium est, nudare inter gives corpora,"
["To strip the body before others is the beginning of wickedness." — Ennius, in Cicero, Tusc. Quaes., iv. 33.]
should have remembered that, as in the mysteries of the Bona Dea every masculine appearance was excluded, he did nothing if he did not also geld horses and donkeys — in short, all of nature:
"Omne adeo genus in terris, hominumque, ferarumque, Et genus aequoreum, pecudes, pictaeque volucres, In furias ignemque ruunt."
["So every kind of living thing on earth — men, beasts, wild or tame, fish, and gaudy fowl — rush to this flame of love." — Virgil, Georg., iii. 244.]

The gods, Plato says, have given us one disobedient and unruly member that, like a furious animal, attempts by the violence of its appetite to subject everything to it; and they have given to women one like a greedy and ravenous animal, which, if refused food in season, grows wild, impatient of delay, and infusing its rage into their bodies, blocks the passages, hinders breathing, and causes a thousand ills, until, having drunk in the fruit of the common thirst, it has plentifully bedewed the bottom of their matrix. Now my legislator might have considered that perhaps it would be a chaster and more fruitful course to let them know the fact as it is, in good time, rather than allow them to guess according to the liberty and heat of their own fancy. In place of the real parts, they substitute, through hope and desire, others that are three times more outsized; and a certain friend of mine ruined himself by producing his in the wrong place and at the wrong time. What harm those pictures of prodigious proportions do that the boys make on the stairs and galleries of the royal houses — they give the ladies a cruel contempt for our natural furniture. And how do we know but that Plato, after other well-ordered republics, decreed that men and women, old and young, should expose themselves naked to each other's view in his gymnastic exercises, on that very account? The Indian women who see the men in their natural state have at least cooled the sense of sight. And let the women of the kingdom of Pegu say what they will — they who below the waist have nothing to cover them but a cloth slit at the front, and so narrow that whatever decency and modesty they pretend by it, at every step everything is to be seen — it is an invention to draw the men to them and divert them from boys, to whom that nation is generally inclined. Yet perhaps they lose more by it than they gain, and one may venture to say that a whole appetite is sharper than one already half-glutted by the eyes. Livia used to say that to a virtuous woman, a naked man was only a statue. The Spartan women, more virgins as wives than our daughters are, saw every day the young men of their city stripped naked in their exercises, and themselves bothered little to cover their thighs in walking, believing themselves, as Plato says, sufficiently covered by their virtue, without any other robe. But those of whom St Augustine speaks have given nudity a wonderful power of temptation, who have made it a question whether women at the day of judgment will rise again in their own sex and not rather in ours, for fear of tempting us again even in that holy state. In short, we lure them and stir them up by every kind of means; we ceaselessly heat and stir up their imagination, and then we find fault. Let us confess the truth: there is scarcely one of us who does not more fear the shame that comes to him from his wife's vices than from his own, and is not more solicitous — wonderful charity! — about the conscience of his virtuous wife than about his own; who would not rather commit theft and sacrilege, and that his wife was a murderess and a heretic, than that she should not be more chaste than her husband. An unjust assessment of vices. Both we and they are capable of a thousand corruptions more harmful and unnatural than lust; but we weigh vices not according to nature, but according to our interest, by which they take so many unequal shapes.

The austerity of our decrees makes women's application to this vice more violent and vicious than its own nature requires, and entangles it in worse consequences than its causes warranted. They will readily go off to the courts to seek gain, or to the wars to win reputation, rather than, in the midst of ease and pleasures, have to mount such a difficult guard. Do they not see well enough that there is neither merchant nor soldier who will not leave his business to run after this sport — nor any porter or cobbler, however tired and worn down by labour and hunger?

"Num tu, qux tenuit dives Achaemenes, Aut pinguis Phrygiae Mygdonias opes, Permutare velis crine Licymnim? Plenas aut Arabum domos, Dum fragrantia detorquet ad oscula Cervicem, aut facili sxvitia negat, Quae poscente magis gaudeat eripi, Interdum rapere occupet?"

["Would you not exchange all that wealthy Achaemenes had, or the Mygdonian riches of fertile Phrygia, for one ringlet of Licymnia's hair? Or the treasures of the Arabians, when she turns her head to you for fragrant kisses, or with easily appeased anger denies them — which she would rather you took by force, and sometimes herself snatches first?" — Horace, Od., ii. 12, 21.]

I do not know whether the exploits of Alexander and Caesar really surpass the resolution of a beautiful young woman, brought up after our fashion in the daylight and traffic of the world, assailed by so many contrary examples, and still keeping herself entire in the midst of a thousand continual and powerful solicitations. There is no doing more difficult than that not-doing, nor more active.
I hold it easier to carry a suit of armour all the days of one's life than a maidenhead; and the vow of virginity is the noblest of all, as being the hardest to keep:
"Diaboli virtus in lumbis est,"

St Jerome says. We have, without doubt, given over to the ladies the most difficult and most strenuous of all human endeavours; let us give them the glory of it too. This ought to encourage them to be obstinate in it; it is a brave thing for them to defy us, and to spurn underfoot that vain pre-eminence of valour and virtue that we claim over them. They will find, if they notice it, that they will not only be much more esteemed for it but also much more loved. A gallant man does not give up his pursuit because he has been refused, provided it is a refusal of chastity and not of personal choice. We may swear, threaten, and complain all we like — we are only lying; we love them all the better for it. There is no allurement like modesty, if it is not rude and sour. It is stupidity and meanness to be stubborn in the face of hatred and disdain; but against a virtuous and constant resolution mixed with goodwill, that is the exercise of a noble and generous soul. They may acknowledge our service to a certain degree and give us civilly to understand that they do not disdain us; for the law that commands them to abhor us because we adore them, and to hate us because we love them, is certainly very cruel — if only for the difficulty of it. Why should they not lend an ear to our offers and requests, so long as they are kept within the bounds of modesty? Why should we imagine them to have other thoughts within, and to be worse than they seem? A queen of our time said wittily that to refuse these courtesies is a sign of weakness in women, and a self-accusation of being easy; and that a lady could not boast of her chastity who had never been tempted.

The limits of honour are not cut so short; they may give themselves a little rein and relax a little without being at fault: there lies on the frontier some space free, indifferent, and neutral. Whoever has beaten and pursued her into her fort is a strange fellow if he is not satisfied with his luck; the price of the conquest is reckoned by the difficulty. Would you know what impression your service and merit have made on her heart? Judge by her behaviour. Such a woman may grant more, who does not grant as much. The obligation of a favour relates wholly to the goodwill of those who confer it; the other circumstances that go with it are mute, dead, and accidental; it costs her dearer to grant you that little than it would cost her companion to grant everything. If rarity gives value to anything, it ought especially to in this; do not consider how little is given, but how few have it to give. The value of money changes according to the coinage and stamp of the place. Whatever the spite and indiscretion of some may make them say in the excess of their discontent, virtue and truth will in time recover all the advantage. I have known some whose reputation has long suffered under slander, who have afterwards been restored to universal approval by their mere constancy, without care or artifice; everyone repents and contradicts what he had believed and said, and women a little suspected as girls have afterward been advanced to the first rank among ladies of honour. Somebody told Plato that all the world spoke ill of him. "Let them talk," he said. "I will live in such a way as to make them change their tune." Besides the fear of God and the value of so rare a glory, which ought to make them look to themselves, the corruption of the age we live in compels them to it; if I were they, there is nothing I would not sooner do than entrust my reputation to such dangerous hands. In my time, the pleasure of telling — a pleasure little inferior to that of doing — was permitted only to those who had some faithful, single friend; but now ordinary conversation and common table-talk is nothing but boasts of favours received and of the secret generosity of ladies. In earnest, it is too abject, too mean-spirited, in men to allow such ungrateful, indiscreet, and giddy people so to persecute, forage, and pillage those tender and charming favours.
This our immoderate and illegitimate exasperation against this vice springs from the most vain and tumultuous disease that afflicts human minds, which is jealousy:
"Quis vetat apposito lumen de lumine sumi? Dent licet assidue, nil tamen inde perit;"
["Who says that one light should not be lighted from another light? Let them give ever so much; as much always remains to lose." — Ovid, De Arte Amandi, iii. 93.]

she and envy, her sister, seem to me the most foolish of the whole troop. Of envy I can say little; it is a passion that, though said to be so mighty and powerful, has never had anything to do with me. As for the other, I know it by sight, and that is all. Beasts feel it. The shepherd Cratis, having fallen in love with a she-goat, was found one day by the he-goat — out of jealousy — and the he-goat butted his head as he lay asleep, and crushed it. We have raised this fever to a greater extreme by the examples of some barbarous nations; the best-disciplined have felt it too, and rightly, but not been carried away by it:
"Ense maritali nemo confossus adulter Purpureo Stygias sanguine tinxit aquas."
Never did an adulterer slain by a husband stain the Stygian waters with purple blood.

Lucullus, Caesar, Pompey, Antony, Cato, and other brave men were cuckolds, and knew it without making any fuss about it. In those days there was only one fool, Lepidus, who died of grief because his wife had treated him so.
"Ah! tum te miserum malique fati, Quem attractis pedibus, patente porta, Percurrent raphanique mugilesque:"
["Ah, wretched man of evil fate! when, taken in the act, you will be dragged out by the heels, and suffer the adulterer's punishment." — Catullus, xv. 17.]
And the god in our poet, when he caught one of his companions with his wife, contented himself with putting them to shame,
"Atque aliquis de dis non tristibus optat Sic fieri turpis:"
["And one of the more cheerful gods wishes he himself might be so disgraced." — Ovid, Metam., iv. 187.]
and nonetheless took offence at the lukewarm embraces she gave him, complaining that on that account she had grown jealous of his affection:
"Quid causas petis ex alto? fiducia cessit Quo tibi, diva, mei?"
["Why do you seek causes from on high? Goddess, where has your confidence in me gone?" — Virgil, Aeneid, viii. 395.]
Indeed she begs arms for a bastard of hers,
"Arena rogo genitrix nato."
["I, a mother, ask armour for a son." — Idem, ibid., 383.]
which are freely granted; and Vulcan speaks honourably of Aeneas:
"Arma acri facienda viro,"
["Arms must be made for a brave hero." — Aeneid, viii. 441.]
with, in truth, a more than human humanity. And I am content to leave this excess of kindness to the gods:
"Nec divis homines componier aequum est."
["Nor is it right to compare men with gods." — Catullus, lxviii. 141.]
As for the confusion of children, besides that the gravest legislators decree and approve it in their republics, it does not trouble the women, in whom this passion is, somehow, much better seated:
"Saepe etiam Juno, maxima coelicolam, Conjugis in culpa flagravit quotidiana."
["Often even Juno, greatest of the dwellers in heaven, was enraged by her husband's daily infidelities." — Idem, ibid.]

When jealousy seizes these poor souls, weak and incapable of resistance, it is a pity to see how miserably it torments and tyrannises over them; it slips in under the title of friendship, but once it has possessed them, the same causes that served as the foundation of goodwill now serve as the foundation of mortal hatred. Of all the diseases of the mind, it is the one that the most things serve to feed and the fewest to relieve. The virtue, health, merit, and reputation of the husband are kindling for her fury and ill-will:
"Nullae sunt inimicitiae, nisi amoris, acerbae."
["No hatreds are bitter except those of love." — Propertius, ii. 8, 3.]

This fever defaces and corrupts everything beautiful and good in her besides; and there is no action of a jealous woman, however chaste and however good a housewife she may be, that does not taste of anger and wrangling. It is a furious agitation, which throws her into an extremity quite opposite to its cause. This held good with one Octavius at Rome. After lying with Pontia Posthumia, he found his love grew by the enjoyment, and importuned her with every plea to marry him; unable to persuade her, this excessive affection threw him headlong into the effects of the most cruel and mortal hatred: he killed her. In the same way, the ordinary symptoms of this other amorous disease are internal hatreds, private conspiracies, and intrigues:
"Notumque furens quid faemina possit,"
["And it is known what a furious woman can do." — Aeneid, v. 21.]
and a rage which frets itself the more, as it is forced to excuse itself under the pretence of goodwill.

Now, the duty of chastity is of vast extent. Is it the will we want them to restrain? That is a very supple and active thing, very nimble and hard to bring to a stop. What if dreams sometimes carry them off so far they cannot refuse? It is not in them, nor perhaps in chastity itself, since chastity is feminine, to defend itself from lust and desire. If we are only to trust to their will, what a case are we in then? Just imagine what a crowd of men would be in pursuit of the privilege to run full speed, without tongue or eyes, into the arms of any woman who would have them. The Scythian women put out the eyes of all their slaves and prisoners of war, so they might have their pleasure of them without their being any the wiser. Oh, the furious advantage of opportunity! If anyone should ask me what is the first thing to be considered in matters of love, I would say it is how to take a fitting time; and the second; and the third — it is a point that does everything. I have sometimes lacked fortune, but sometimes I have been lacking to myself in matters of attempt. God help the man who still makes light of this. There is greater rashness required in our age — something our young men excuse under the name of heat; but should women examine it more strictly, they would find it springs from contempt rather. I was always superstitiously afraid of giving offence, and have always had great respect for the one I loved; besides, whoever takes away the reverence in this traffic also defaces the lustre. I would have a man, in this affair, be a little childish, a little timorous, a little servile. If not in this, I have in other matters something of that bashfulness Plutarch speaks of, and the course of my life has been damaged and blemished by it in various ways — a quality very ill-suited to my general make-up; and what are we, indeed, but contradiction and inconsistency? I am as much out of countenance to be denied as I am to deny; and it troubles me so much to put others to trouble that, on occasions when duty obliges me to test the goodwill of any one of them in a doubtful matter that will be a burden to him, I do it very faintly and very much against the grain. But if it is for my own particular interest (whatever Homer truly says, that modesty is a foolish virtue in a needy person), I commonly commit it to a third person to blush for me, and to refuse those who employ me with the same reluctance. So that it has sometimes happened that I had a mind to refuse but lacked the power to do it.

It is folly, then, to try to bridle in women a desire so powerful in them and so natural to them. And when I hear them boast of having such a maidenly and temperate will, I laugh at them. They retire too far back. If it is an old toothless hag, or a young dried-up consumptive thing, though it may not be wholly believable, at least they say it with some plausibility. But those who still move and breathe, talking at that ridiculous rate, do so to their own prejudice — because inconsiderate excuses are a kind of self-accusation. Like a gentleman, a neighbour of mine, suspected of impotence:
"Languidior tenera cui pendens sicula beta, Numquam se mediam sustulit ad tunicam,"
[Catullus, lxvii. 2, i. — The sense is given by the context.]

who, three or four days after he was married, went around boldly swearing, to clear himself, that he had ridden twenty stages the previous night — an oath that was afterwards used to convict him of his unfitness in that affair, and to divorce him from his wife. Besides, it means nothing, for there is neither continence nor virtue where there are no opposing desires. It is true, they may say, but we will not yield. Saints themselves speak in that manner — I mean those who boast in good gravity of their coldness and insensibility, and expect to be believed with a serious face. For when it is spoken with an affected look, when their eyes give the lie to their tongue, and when they talk in the cant of their profession, which always goes against the grain, it is rare sport. I am a great servant of liberty and plainness, but there is no remedy: if it is not wholly simple or childish, it is silly and unbecoming to ladies in this commerce, and runs straightaway into impudence. Their disguises and figures only serve to fool fools; lying is there in its seat of honour. It is a back-way that, by a side-door, leads us to truth. If we cannot curb their imagination, what do we want from them? Their actions? There are plenty of those that evade all outside communication, by which chastity may be corrupted:
"Illud saepe facit, quod sine teste facit;"
["He often does that which he does without a witness." — Martial, vii. 62, 6.]
and those we fear least are perhaps most to be feared; the sins that make the least noise are the worst:
"Offendor maecha simpliciore minus."
["I am less offended by an open-living strumpet." — Idem, vi. 7, 6.]
There are ways by which they may lose their virginity without prostitution, and, what is more, without their own knowledge:
"Obsterix, virginis cujusdam integritatem manu velut explorans, sive malevolentia, sive inscitia, sive casu, dum inspicit, perdidit."
["By malevolence, or unskilfulness, or accident, the midwife, while testing some maiden's virginity with her hand, has sometimes destroyed it." — St Augustine, De Civit. Dei, i. 18.]

Such a one, looking for her maidenhead, has lost it; another, playing with it, has destroyed it. We cannot precisely circumscribe the actions we forbid; they must guess at our meaning under general and doubtful terms. The very idea we invent of their chastity is ridiculous: among the highest patterns I have is Fatua, the wife of Faunus, who, after her marriage, never again let herself be seen by any man whatever; and the wife of Hiero, who never noticed her husband's stinking breath, imagining it common to all men. They have to become insensible and invisible to satisfy us.

Now, let us confess that the knot of this judgment of duty principally lies in the will. There have been husbands who suffered cuckoldom not only without reproach or taking offence at their wives, but with a sense of being singularly obliged to them, and great praise of their virtue. There has been such a woman, who valued her honour above her life, and yet has prostituted it to the raging lust of a mortal enemy to save her husband's life, and who, in so doing, did that for him she would not have done for herself. This is not the place to multiply such examples; they are too high and rich to be set off with so poor a foil as I can give them here; let us save them for a nobler place. But for examples of ordinary lustre, do we not see every day women among us who surrender themselves for their husbands' sole benefit, by their husbands' express order and mediation? And of old, Phaulius the Argive, who offered his wife to King Philip out of ambition; or Galba, who did it out of courtesy: having entertained Maecenas at supper, and noticing that his wife and Maecenas began to cast glances at each other and to exchange signs, Galba let himself sink down on his cushion like a man in a deep sleep, to give their desires their chance — which he handsomely admitted, for when a servant made bold to lay hands on some plate on the table, he cried out frankly, "What, you rogue? Don't you see that I am only sleeping for Maecenas?" There may be such, whose manners may be lewd enough but whose will is more upright than another's, who outwardly behaves more regularly. And we see some who complain of having vowed chastity before they knew what they did, and I have known others actually complain of having been given over to debauchery before they had reached the years of discretion. The vice of the parents, or the urge of nature — which is a rough counsellor — may be the cause.

In the East Indies, though chastity was held in singular reputation, custom permitted a married woman to prostitute herself to anyone who presented her with an elephant — and that to her glory, to have been valued at such a high price. Phaedo the philosopher, a man of birth, after the taking of his country, Elis, made it his trade to prostitute the beauty of his youth, so long as it lasted, to anyone who would pay him, in order to earn a living. And Solon was the first in Greece, it is said, to give women, by his laws, liberty to provide for the needs of life at the expense of their chastity — a custom that Herodotus says had been received in many states before his time. And anyway, what is the fruit of all this painful watching? For however just this passion may be, we still have to consider whether it gets us anywhere. Does anyone think to curb them, with all his ingenuity?
"Pone seram; cohibe: sed quis custodiet ipsos Custodes? cauta est, et ab illis incipit uxor."
["Put a lock on her; shut her up under a guard; but who shall guard the guards? Your wife is shrewd, and begins with them." — Juvenal, vi. 346.]
What kind of commodity will not serve their turn in such a knowing age?

Curiosity is vicious in general; but it is pernicious here. It is folly to investigate a disease for which there is no medicine that doesn't inflame and worsen it; whose shame grows still greater and more public through jealousy; and whose revenge wounds our children more than it heals us. You wither and die in the search for so obscure a proof. How miserably have those of my time arrived at such knowledge who have been unhappy enough to find it out! If the informer does not at the same time apply a remedy and bring relief, his information is harmful, and rather deserves a stab than a flat lie. We laugh as much at the man who labours to prevent it as at the man who is a cuckold and doesn't know it. The mark of cuckold is indelible; whoever once carries it carries it to his grave; the punishment proclaims it more than the fault. It is much to drag our private misfortunes out of obscurity and doubt, only to expose them on tragic scaffolds; misfortunes that hurt us only by being known. We say a woman is a good wife, or a marriage is happy, not because they really are so, but because no one says the contrary. Men should be wise enough to evade this tormenting and useless knowledge — and the Romans had a custom, when returning from any expedition, of sending home a messenger ahead to let their wives know of their coming, so they would not surprise them. And for this reason a certain nation has introduced the custom that on the wedding-day the priest shall open the way for the bride, to free the husband from the doubt and curiosity of examining, at the first assault, whether she comes a virgin to his bed or has been at the trade before.

But the world will be talking. I know a hundred honest men cuckolds, honestly and not unbecomingly. A worthy man is pitied for it, not held in less esteem. Order it so that your virtue overcomes your misfortune, that good men curse the occasion, and that he who wrongs you trembles only to think of it. Besides, who escapes being talked of in the same way, from the least to the greatest?
"Tot qui legionibus imperitivit Et melior quam to multis fuit, improbe, rebus."
["Many who have commanded legions, many a man much better than you, you rascal." — Lucretius, iii. 1039, 1041.]

Do you see how many honest men in your hearing are reproached with this? Then believe that you are no more spared elsewhere. But — even the ladies will laugh. And what are they so quick to laugh at in this virtuous age of ours as a peaceable and well-composed marriage? Each one of you has made somebody a cuckold; nature runs much in parallel, by compensation, turn for turn. The frequency of this accident ought long since to have made it more bearable; it has now passed into custom.
Miserable passion, which has this on top of everything else, that it cannot be shared:
"Fors etiam nostris invidit questibus aures;"
["Fortune itself refuses an ear to our complaints." — Catullus, lxvii.]

For to what friend dare you entrust your griefs, who, even if he doesn't laugh at them, won't make use of the occasion to get a share of the spoils? The bitterness, as well as the sweets, of marriage is kept secret by the wise; and among its other troublesome conditions, to a chatterer like me, this is one of the chief: that custom has made it indecent and prejudicial to communicate to anyone everything a man knows and feels. To give women the same counsel against jealousy would be so much time lost; their very being is so made up of suspicion, vanity, and curiosity that to cure them by any legitimate way is not to be hoped. They often recover from this infirmity by a kind of health more to be feared than the disease itself; for as there are enchantments which can only take away the evil by throwing it onto another, they will willingly transfer this one to their husbands when they shake it off themselves. And yet I do not know, to tell the truth, whether a man can suffer worse from them than their jealousy; it is the most dangerous of all their conditions, as the head is of all their members. Pittacus used to say that everyone had his trouble, and that his was his wife's jealous head; but for that, he would think himself perfectly happy. A mighty inconvenience, indeed, that could poison the whole life of so just, so wise, and so valiant a man — what must we lesser fellows do? The senate of Marseilles was right to grant his request to the man who begged leave to kill himself so he might be delivered from the clamour of his wife — for it is a misfortune that is never got rid of except by getting rid of the whole piece, and has no remedy but flight or patience, both of them very hard. It was, I think, an understanding man who said it was a happy marriage between a blind wife and a deaf husband.

Let us also consider whether the great and violent severity of obligation we impose on them does not produce two effects contrary to our design — that is, whether it does not make their pursuers more eager to attack, and the women more easy to yield. For as to the first, by raising the value of the place, we raise the value and desire of the conquest. Could it not be Venus herself who so cunningly raised the price of her merchandise by making the laws her procurers, knowing how flat a delight it would be that was not heightened by fancy and difficulty? In short, it is all pork, varied by sauces, as Flaminius' host said. Cupid is a roguish god who makes it his sport to contend with devotion and justice; it is his glory that his power outmatches all other powers, and that all other rules give place to his:
"Materiam culpae prosequiturque suae."
["And he seeks out a motive for his crimes." — Ovid, Trist., iv. 1. 34.]
As to the second point: should we not be less cuckolds if we less feared to be so — given the humour of women, whom prohibition incites and who are made more eager by being forbidden?
"Ubi velis, nolunt; ubi nolis, volunt ultro; Concessa pudet ire via."
["Where you want them to, they will not; where you do not want them to, they spontaneously agree; they are ashamed to go on the permitted road." — Terence, Eunuchus, act iv., sc. 8, v. 43.]

What better interpretation can we make of Messalina's behaviour? At first she made her husband a cuckold in private, as is the common practice; but, bringing her business about with too much ease, because of her husband's stupidity, she soon scorned that path and presently fell to making open love, to acknowledging her lovers, and to favouring and entertaining them in the sight of everyone. She wanted him to know it, to see it. The animal would not be roused by any of it, and made her pleasures dull and flat by his too-stupid acquiescence, by which he seemed to authorise and legitimate them — so what does she do? While she is the wife of a living and healthy emperor, in Rome, the theatre of the world, in the face of the sun and with solemn ceremony, she publicly marries Silius, who had long before enjoyed her, one day when her husband was out of town. Doesn't it look as if she meant to become chaste through her husband's negligence, or that she was looking for another husband who might sharpen her appetite by his jealousy, and incite her by watching her? But the first difficulty she met with was also the last; this beast was suddenly roused. These sleepy, sluggish men are often the most dangerous. I have found by experience that this extreme toleration, when it does dissolve, produces the most severe revenge: catching fire all at once, anger and fury combined into one, it discharges its utmost force at the first attack,
"Irarumque omnes effundit habenas:"
["He let loose all the reins of his fury." — Aeneid, xii. 499.]
he put her to death, along with a great number of those with whom she had had dealings, including even one who could not help himself, and whom she had had forced to her bed under the whip.
What Virgil says of Venus and Vulcan, Lucretius has expressed better, in a stolen enjoyment between Venus and Mars:

"Belli fera moenera Mavors Armipotens regit, ingremium qui saepe tuum se Rejictt, aeterno devinctus vulnere amoris ... Pascit amore avidos inhians in te, Dea, visus, Eque tuo pendet resupini spiritus ore Hunc tu, Diva, tuo recubantem corpore sancto Circumfusa super, suaveis ex ore loquelas Funde."

["Mars, the god of wars who controls the cruel labours of war, often reclines on your bosom, vanquished by the eternal wound of love, and there feeds his greedy gaze upon you, goddess, drinking love at his eyes; and as he lies back, his breath hangs upon your lips. Pour forth, divine one, sweet persuasive words, encircling him as he lies upon your sacred person." — Lucretius, i. 23.]

When I consider those words — rejicit, pascit, inhians, molli, fovet, medullas, labefacta, pendet, percurrit — and that splendid circumfusa, mother of the pretty infusus — I scorn those little quibbles and verbal allusions that have sprung up since. Those worthy men needed no subtlety to disguise their meaning; their language is downright, full of natural unbroken vigour. They are all epigram, not just the tail, but the head, body, and feet too. There is nothing forced, nothing languishing; everything keeps the same pace:
"Contextus totes virilis est; non sunt circa flosculos occupati."
["The whole texture is manly; they do not busy themselves about little flowers of rhetoric." — Seneca, Ep., 33.]

It is not a soft eloquence, and merely inoffensive; it is sinewy and solid, and does not so much please as fill and ravish the greatest minds. When I see these brave forms of expression, so lively, so deep, I do not say it is well said but well thought. It is the liveliness of the imagination that swells and lifts the words:
"Pectus est quod disertum Tacit."
["The heart is what makes a man eloquent." — Quintilian, x. 7.]

Our people call language, judgment, and fine words "full conceptions." This painting is done not so much by dexterity of hand as by having the object more vividly imprinted on the soul. Gallus speaks simply because he conceives simply. Horace does not content himself with a superficial expression — that would betray him; he sees farther and more clearly into things; his mind breaks into and rummages through the whole storehouse of words and figures with which to express himself, and they have to be out of the ordinary, because his conception is so. Plutarch says he sees the Latin tongue through the things; here it is the same; the sense illuminates and brings forth the words — no more words of air, but of flesh and bone; they signify more than they say. Even those who are not very skilled in a language give us some image of this; for in Italy I said whatever I had a mind to in common conversation, but in more serious talk I would not have trusted myself to an idiom I could not wind and turn out of its ordinary pace. I want to have the power of introducing something of my own.

The handling and utterance of fine wits is what gives language its lustre; not so much by innovating in it as by putting it to more vigorous and various services, and by straining, bending, and adapting it to them. They do not create words, but they enrich their own, and give them weight and meaning by the uses they put them to, teaching them unaccustomed motions — but with ingenuity and discretion. And how little this talent is given to all is shown by the many French scribblers of this age: they are bold and proud enough not to follow the common road, but want of invention and discretion ruins them. There is nothing in their writings but a wretched affectation of a strange new style, with cold absurd disguises, which, instead of elevating, depress the matter. Provided they can deck themselves out with new words, they don't care what they signify; and to bring in a new word by the scruff of the neck, they will leave the old one, often sinewier and more meaningful than the new.

There is stuff enough in our language, but there is a defect in how we cut it up; for there is nothing that might not be made out of our terms of hunting and war, which is a rich soil to borrow from; and forms of speaking, like herbs, improve and grow stronger by being transplanted. I find our language sufficiently abundant but not sufficiently pliable and vigorous; it commonly quails under a powerful conception. If you would maintain the dignity of your style, you will often see it flag and languish under you, and there Latin steps in to help, as Greek does for others. Of some of these words I have just picked out, we do not so easily perceive the energy, because their frequent use has somewhat lowered their beauty and made them common — just as in our ordinary language there are many excellent phrases and metaphors whose beauty has withered with age, and whose colour has been sullied by too common handling. But that takes nothing from the relish for them in a discerning man's eyes, nor does it diminish the glory of those ancient authors who, in all likelihood, first brought those words into that lustre.

The sciences treat of things too subtly, in an artificial way, very different from the common and natural one. My page makes love, and understands it; but read him Leo Hebraeus or Ficino, where they speak of love, its thoughts and actions, and he will not understand it. I do not find most of my ordinary motions in Aristotle; they are there covered and disguised in another robe, for the use of the schools. Good luck to them — were I of the trade, I would as much naturalise art as they artificialise nature. Let us leave Bembo and Equicola alone.

When I write, I can very well spare both the company and the memory of books, lest they interrupt my progress; and indeed, the best authors too much humble and discourage me. I am very much of the painter's mind who, having painted cocks very poorly, ordered all his apprentices not to allow any natural cock to come into his shop; and I would rather need to give myself a little lustre by the device of Antigenides the musician, who, when he was asked to sing or play, took care beforehand that the audience should, either before or after, be glutted with some other bad musician. But I can hardly do without Plutarch; he is so universal and so full that on every occasion, and on whatever extravagant subject you take in hand, he will be at your elbow, holding out a generous and inexhaustible hand of riches and embellishments. It vexes me that he is so exposed to be pillaged by those who frequent him; I can scarcely cast an eye over him without stealing either a leg or a wing.

And so for this design of mine, it is convenient for me to write at home, in a wild country where I have no one to assist me or relieve me, where I hardly meet a man who understands the Latin of his Paternoster, and of French somewhat less. I might have made the book better elsewhere, but then the work would have been less mine; and its chief end and perfection is to be exactly mine. I readily correct an accidental error, of which I am full, since I run carelessly on; but for my ordinary and constant imperfections, it would be a kind of treason to remove them. When someone tells me, or I tell myself, "You are too thick with figures: this is a word of rough Gascon: that is a dangerous phrase" (I do not reject any of those used in the common streets of France; those who would fight custom with grammar are triflers): "this is an ignorant discourse, that a paradoxical one; this is going too far; you make yourself too merry at times; people will think you say a thing in good earnest that you only say in jest" — "Yes, I know, but I correct only the faults of inadvertence, not those of custom. Do I not talk at the same rate throughout? Do I not represent myself to the life? It is enough that I have done what I designed; the whole world knows me in my book, and my book in me."

Now I have an apish, imitative quality: when I used to write verses (and I only ever wrote them in Latin), they obviously betrayed the poet I had last read, and some of my first essays have a little exotic taste. I speak rather a different kind of language at Paris than I do at Montaigne. Whoever I look at steadily easily leaves some impression of himself on me; whatever I observe I usurp, whether it be a foolish countenance, an unpleasant look, or a ridiculous way of speaking; and vices most of all, because they seize hold of me and stick, and will not let go without shaking. I swear more by imitation than by complexion: a murderous imitation, like that of the apes — so terrible in stature and strength — that Alexander met with in a certain country of the Indies and which he would have had much trouble subduing any other way; but they offered him the means by their inclination to imitate everything they saw done. By this the hunters were taught to put on shoes in the apes' sight, and to tie them tight with many knots, and to muffle up their heads in caps made all of running nooses, and to seem to anoint their eyes with glue; so did those poor beasts use their imitation to their own ruin — they glued up their own eyes, haltered and bound themselves. The other faculty of playing the mimic, ingeniously acting the words and gestures of another to amuse people and raise their admiration, is no more in me than in a stock. When I swear my own oath, it is only "By God!" — the most direct of all oaths. They say Socrates swore by the dog; Zeno used the same interjection now in use among the Italians, "Cappari!"; Pythagoras swore by water and air. I am so apt, without thinking of it, to take on these superficial impressions, that if I have "Majesty" or "Highness" in my mouth three days running, they come out instead of "Excellency" and "Lordship" a week later; and what I say today in sport and fooling I shall say tomorrow in earnest. So in writing I more unwillingly take up beaten arguments, lest I should handle them at someone else's expense. Every subject is equally fertile to me; a fly will serve the purpose; and it is well if what I have in hand has not been taken up at the prompting of an equally flighty whim. I may begin with whatever pleases me best, for the subjects are all linked to one another.

But my soul displeases me in that it ordinarily produces its deepest and most airy notions, which please me most, when I least expect or look for them; and they vanish all at once, with nothing to fix them on — on horseback, at table, or in bed, but most on horseback, where I am most given to thinking. My speech is a little jealous of silence and attention: if I am talking my best, whoever interrupts me stops me. Travelling, the demands of the road will often put a stop to discourse; besides which, I generally travel without company fit for regular conversation, so that I have all the leisure I want to entertain myself. It falls out as in my dreams: while dreaming I commend them to my memory (I am apt to dream that I am dreaming), but the next morning I can recall what colour they were — gay, or sad, or strange — but as to the rest, the more I try to retrieve them, the deeper I plunge them into oblivion. So with thoughts that come accidentally into my head: I have no more than a vain image left in my memory, just enough to make me torment myself in trying to find them again, to no purpose.

Well, then, laying books aside and speaking more simply and materially, I find, when all is done, that Love is nothing but the thirst of enjoying the object desired, or that Venus is nothing but the pleasure of discharging one's vessels — just as the pleasure nature gives in discharging the other parts, which by immoderation or indiscretion become vicious. According to Socrates, love is the appetite for generation through the mediation of beauty. And when I consider the ridiculous tickling of this pleasure, the absurd, crack-brained, wild motions with which it inspires Zeno and Cratippus, the indiscreet rage, the countenance inflamed with fury and cruelty in the sweetest effects of love, and then that austere, grave, severe, ecstatic air in so wanton an action; that our delights and our excrements are promiscuously shuffled together; and that the supreme pleasure brings with it, like pain, fainting and complaining; I believe it to be true, as Plato says, that the gods made man for their sport:
"Quaenam ista jocandi Saevitia!"
["What an unkindness there is in jesting!" — Claudian, in Eutrop. i. 24.]

and that it was in mockery that nature ordered the most agitating of actions, and the most common, to make us equal, and to put fools and wise men, beasts and us, on a level. Even the most contemplative and prudent man, when I imagine him in this posture, I hold an impudent fellow for pretending to be prudent and contemplative; these are the peacock's feet that lower his pride:
"Ridentem dicere verum Quid vetat?"
["What prevents one from telling the truth with a smile?" — Horace, Sat., i. 1, 24.]

Those who banish serious thoughts from their sports, says someone, are like a man who dares not adore the statue of a saint unless it is covered with a veil. We eat and drink, indeed, as the beasts do; but these are not actions that obstruct the soul's functions; in these we keep our advantage over them. This other action subjects every other thought, and by its imperious authority makes an ass of all Plato's divinity and philosophy; and yet no one complains of it. In every other thing a man may keep some decorum; all other operations submit to the rules of decency; this one cannot, even in imagination, appear anything but vicious or ridiculous. Find out, if you can, any serious, discreet procedure in it. Alexander said that what chiefly let him know he was mortal was this act and sleeping; sleep stifles and suppresses the soul's faculties, and the company of women likewise dissipates and exhausts them. Without a doubt, it is a mark not only of our original corruption but of our vanity and deformity.

On the one hand, nature pushes us into it, having fixed the most noble, useful, and pleasant of all her functions to this desire; and on the other, leaves us to accuse it and shun it, as if it were insolent and indecent, to blush at it, and to recommend abstinence. Are we not brutes to call brutish the work that begets us? Peoples of so many differing religions have agreed on various rites — sacrifices, lamps, burning incense, fasts, offerings — and among others in condemning this act; all opinions tend that way, besides the widespread custom of circumcision, which can be looked on as a punishment. We have perhaps reason to blame ourselves for being guilty of so foolish a production as man, and to call the act and the parts that perform the act shameful (mine, in truth, are now shameful and pitiful). The Essenes, whom Pliny speaks of, sustained their country for several ages without nurse or baby-clothes, by the arrival of strangers who, taking up this odd humour, kept coming to join them; a whole nation resolved to hazard total extermination rather than engage in female embraces, and to lose the succession of men rather than beget one. They say that Zeno only had to do with a woman once in his life, and then out of civility, that he might not seem too obstinately to scorn the sex.
[Diogenes Laertius, vii. 13. What is said there, however, is that Zeno seldom had commerce with boys, lest he be thought a complete misogynist.]

Everyone avoids seeing a man born; everyone runs to see him die. To destroy a man, a spacious field is sought out in the face of the sun; but to make one, we creep into as dark and private a corner as we can; it is a man's duty to withdraw bashfully from the light to create, but it is glory and the fountain of many virtues to know how to destroy what we have made — the one being an injury, the other a favour. For Aristotle says that to do anyone a kindness, in a certain phrase of his country, is to kill him. The Athenians, to couple the disgrace of these two actions, having to purify the isle of Delos and justify themselves to Apollo, banned both births and burials within its precincts:
"Nostri nosmet paenitet."
["We are ashamed of ourselves." — Terence, Phormio, i. 3, 20.]

There are nations that won't be seen to eat. I know a lady, of the best quality, who is of the same opinion — that chewing disfigures the face and takes away much from a lady's grace and beauty, and so unwillingly appears at a public table with an appetite. And I know a man too who cannot endure to see another eat, nor himself to be seen eating; he is more shy of company when putting in than putting out. In the Turkish empire there are a great number of men who, to excel others, never let themselves be seen when they take their meal; who only eat once a week; who cut and gash their faces and limbs; who never speak to anyone — fanatical people who think to honour their nature by denaturing themselves, who value themselves on their contempt of themselves, and propose to grow better by being worse. What monstrous animal is this, who is a horror to himself, to whom his delights are a grief, and who weds himself to misfortune? There are people who conceal their life:
"Exilioque domos et dulcia limina mutant,"
["And they exchange their homes and sweet thresholds for exile." — Virgil, Georg., ii. 511.]

and withdraw from the sight of other men; who avoid health and cheerfulness as dangerous and prejudicial qualities. Not only many sects but many peoples curse their birth and bless their death; and there is a place where the sun is cursed and darkness adored. We are only ingenious in using ourselves ill; it is the real quarry our wits fly at; and the intellect, when misapplied, is a dangerous tool!
"O miseri! quorum gaudia crimen habent!"
["O wretched men, whose pleasures are a crime!" — Pseudo-Gallus, i. 180.]

Alas, poor man! you have enough inevitable inconveniences without increasing them by your own invention, and are wretched enough by nature without being so by art. You have real and essential deformities enough without forging imaginary ones. Do you think you are too much at ease unless half your ease is uneasy? Do you find that you have not performed all the necessary offices nature has laid on you, and that she is idle in you, unless you bind yourself to other new ones? You don't stick at infringing her universal and undoubted laws; but you stick to your own particular and fantastic rules, and the more particular, uncertain, and contradictory they are, the more you employ your whole care on them. The laws of your parish occupy you and bind you; those of God and the world don't concern you. Just run over the examples of this kind a little; your life is full of them.

While the verses of these two poets treat wantonness as reservedly and discreetly as they do, they discover it, it seems to me, much more openly. Ladies cover their necks with netting, priests cover several sacred things, painters shadow their pictures to give them more lustre; and they say that the sun and wind strike more violently by reflection than in a straight line. The Egyptian wisely answered the man who asked him what he had under his cloak: "It is hid under my cloak," he said, "so that you may not know what it is." But there are certain other things that people hide only to show them. Listen to that other, who speaks plainer:
"Et nudum pressi corpus ad usque meum:"
["And pressed her naked body to mine." — Ovid, Amor., i. 5, 24.]

it seems to me he unmans me. Let Martial turn up Venus as high as he can, he cannot show her so naked. He who says everything that is to be said gluts and disgusts us; he who is afraid to express himself draws us on to guess more than is meant. There is a treachery in this kind of modesty, and especially when, like these two, they half open so fair a path to imagination. Both the action and the description ought to taste of theft.

The more respectful, more timorous, more coy, secret love of the Spaniards and Italians pleases me. I don't know who of old wished his throat as long as a crane's, so he could the longer taste what he swallowed; this would have been better wished for as to this quick precipitous pleasure, especially in such natures as mine, that have the fault of being too prompt. To stay its flight, and put off the moment with preambles — every glance, every bow, every word, every sign passes between them for favour and reward. Wouldn't it be excellent thrift in a man who could dine on the steam of the roast? It is a passion that mixes with very little solid substance — far more vanity and feverish raving; and we should serve it and pay it accordingly. Let us teach the ladies to set a better value and esteem on themselves, to amuse us and fool us; we deliver the last charge at the first attack; the French impetuosity will always show itself. By spinning out their favours and giving them out in small parcels, even miserable old age will find some little share of reward, according to its worth and merit. He who finds no pleasure but in the having, who wins nothing unless he sweeps the stakes, who takes no pleasure in the chase but only in the quarry, ought not to enrol himself in our school: the more steps and degrees there are, the higher and more honourable the topmost seat. We should take pleasure in being led to it, as in magnificent palaces, by various porticoes and passages, long pleasant galleries, and many turnings. This arrangement of things would turn to our advantage; we would stay there longer and love longer; without hope and without desire we get nowhere. Our conquest and entire possession is what they ought infinitely to dread; once they surrender themselves wholly to the mercy of our fidelity and constancy, they run a mighty hazard — these are virtues very rare and hard to be found. As soon as the ladies are ours, we are no longer theirs:
"Postquam cupidae mentis satiata libido est, Verba nihil metuere, nihil perjuria curant;"
["Once their desire is satisfied, they fear no oaths and care nothing for promises." — Catullus, lxiv. 147.]

And Thrasonides, a young man of Greece, was so in love with his own passion that, having gained his mistress's consent, he refused to enjoy her, so as not to extinguish and stupefy through fruition the restless ardour he was so proud of and fed himself on. Costliness is a good sauce to a dish: just see how much the manner of greeting peculiar to our nation has, by its easiness, made kisses — which Socrates says are so powerful and dangerous for stealing the heart — of no esteem at all. It is a displeasing custom, and injurious to the ladies, that they have to lend their lips to every fellow with three footmen at his heels, however ill-favoured he may be in himself:
"Cujus livida naribus caninis Dependet glacies, rigetque barba . . . Centum occurrere malo culilingis:" — Martial, vii. 94.

and even we ourselves are scarcely the better for it; for the way the world is divided, for three beautiful women we must kiss fifty ugly ones; and to a tender stomach like those of my age, an ill kiss costs more than a good one is worth.

In Italy they passionately court even their common women, who sell themselves for money, and justify it by saying: "There are degrees of enjoyment, and by this service we secure for ourselves the fullest; the women sell only their bodies; the will is too free and too much its own to be put up for sale." So they say it is the will they are courting, and they have reason. It is indeed the will we are to serve and gain by our wooing. I abhor to imagine to myself a body without affection; and this madness is, I think, cousin to that of the boy who would needs pollute the beautiful statue of Venus made by Praxiteles; or that of the furious Egyptian who violated the dead corpse of a woman he was embalming — which gave rise to the law then made in Egypt that the bodies of beautiful young women and those of good quality should be kept three days before being delivered to those whose office it was to bury them. Periander did more strangely, extending his conjugal affection (more regular and lawful) to the enjoyment of his wife Melissa after she was dead. Doesn't it look like a lunatic humour in the Moon, that, since she could not otherwise enjoy her darling Endymion, she laid him asleep for several months, and pleased herself with the enjoyment of a boy who stirred only in his sleep? I likewise say that we love a body without soul or sentiment when we love a body without its consent and desire. Not all enjoyments are alike: some are hectic and languishing; a thousand other causes besides goodwill may procure us this favour from the ladies; it is not a sufficient testimony of affection; treachery may lurk there as elsewhere; they sometimes go to it by halves:
"Tanquam thura merumque parent Absentem marmoreamve putes:"
["As if they were preparing frankincense and wine . . . you would think her absent or made of marble." — Martial, xi. 103, 12 and 59, 8.]

I know some who would rather lend that than their coach, and who only impart themselves that way. You have to examine whether your company pleases them on any other account, or, as some strong-chined groom, for that only; what degree of favour and esteem you have with them:
"Tibi si datur uni, Quem lapide illa diem candidiore notat."
["That is enough, if that day alone is given to you which she marks with a whiter stone." — Catullus, lxviii. 147.]
What if they eat your bread with the sauce of a more pleasing imagination?
"Te tenet, absentes alios suspirat amores."
["She holds you in her arms; her sighs are for other, absent lovers." — Tibullus, i. 6, 35.]
What? Have we not seen one in our own day who made use of this act for the purpose of a most horrid revenge, killing and poisoning, as he did, a worthy lady by that means?

Those who know Italy will not think it strange that for this subject I look no further for examples; that nation may be called the regent of the world in this. They have more generally good-looking women, and fewer ugly ones, than we do; but for rare and excellent beauties we have as many as they. I think the same of their wits: of the common sort, they have evidently far more — brutishness is incomparably rarer there; but in individual characters of the highest stamp, we owe them nothing. If I should carry the comparison further, I might say, on the other hand, that as to valour, it is, by comparison, common and natural with us; but sometimes we see them possessed of it to a degree that surpasses the greatest examples we can produce. The marriages of that country are defective in this: their custom commonly imposes so harsh and slavish a law on the women that the most distant acquaintance with a stranger is as capital an offence as the most intimate; so that, since all approaches are necessarily made substantial, and since it all comes to one account, they have no hard choice to make; and once they have broken down the fence, we can safely presume they take fire:
"Luxuria ipsis vinculis, sicut fera bestia, irritata, deinde emissa."
["Lust, like a wild beast, made fiercer by its chains, then breaks loose." — Livy, xxxiv. 4.]
They must be given a little more rein:
"Vidi ego nuper equum, contra sua frena tenacem, Ore reluctanti fulminis ire modo":
["I saw, the other day, a horse struggling against his bit, rush off like a thunderbolt." — Ovid, Amor., iii. 4, 13.]

the desire for company is calmed by giving it a little liberty. We are very much in the same case: they are extreme in constraint, we in licence. It is a good custom we have in France that our sons are received into the best families, to be entertained and brought up as pages, in a kind of school of nobility; and it is looked on as a discourtesy and an affront to refuse this to a gentleman. I have noticed (for, as many families, so many differing forms) that the ladies who have been strictest with their maids have had no better luck than those who allowed them greater liberty. There should be moderation in these things; a great deal of their conduct must be left to their own discretion, for, in the end, no discipline can curb them throughout. But it is also true that the woman who comes off with flying colours from a school of liberty brings with her grounds for more confidence than she who comes away sound from a severe and strict school.

Our fathers dressed up their daughters' looks in bashfulness and fear (their courage and desires being the same); we dress ours in confidence and assurance. We understand nothing of the matter. We must leave it to the Sarmatian women, who may not lie with a man until they have killed another in battle with their own hands. As for me, who have no other title left to such things but by the ears, it is enough if, according to the privilege of my age, they keep me on their counsel. I advise them, then, and us men too, to abstinence; but if the age we live in will not endure it, at least to modesty and discretion. For, as in the story of Aristippus, who, speaking to some young men who blushed at seeing him go into a scandalous house, said "The vice is in not coming out, not in going in," let her who has no care for her conscience have at least some regard for her reputation; and though she is rotten within, let her carry a fair outside at least.

I commend a gradual delay in bestowing their favours. Plato declares that, in all sorts of love, easiness and promptness are forbidden to the one being courted. It is a sign of eagerness, which they ought to disguise with all the art they have, so rashly, so wholly, and so over-hand to surrender themselves. In carrying themselves in an orderly, measured way in the granting of their last favours, they much better stir our desires and hide their own. Let them still fly before us, even those who have most mind to be overtaken; they conquer us better by fleeing, as the Scythians did. To tell the truth, according to the law nature has imposed on them, it is not properly for them either to will or to desire; their part is to suffer, obey, and consent; and for this nature has given them a perpetual capacity, where ours is only by fits and uncertain. They are always fit for the encounter, that they may always be ready when we are — "Pati natae." ["Born to suffer." — Seneca, Ep., 95.] And whereas nature has ordered that our appetites be made manifest by a prominent demonstration, she has wanted theirs to be hidden and concealed within, and has furnished them with parts unfit for ostentation, and simply defensive. Such proceedings as the following must be left to Amazonian licence: Alexander marching his army through Hyrcania, Thalestris, queen of the Amazons, came with three hundred light horse of her own sex, well mounted and armed, having left the rest of a very great army that followed her behind the neighbouring mountains, to pay him a visit; where she publicly told him in plain terms that the fame of his valour and victories had brought her there to see him, and to make him an offer of her forces to assist him in the pursuit of his enterprises; and that, finding him so handsome, young, and vigorous, she — who was also perfect in all those qualities — advised that they should lie together, so that from the most valiant woman in the world and the bravest man then living, some great and wonderful issue might spring for the time to come. Alexander thanked her for everything else; but to give time for the accomplishment of her last demand, he detained her thirteen days in that place, which were spent in royal feasting and merriment, for the welcome of so courageous a princess.

We are, almost throughout, unjust judges of their actions, as they are of ours. I confess the truth when it tells against me, as well as when it is on my side. It is an abominable intemperance that drives them so often to change, and that will not let them limit their affection to any one person whatever; as is evident in that goddess to whom so many changes and so many lovers are attributed. But it is also true that it is contrary to the nature of love if it is not violent, and contrary to the nature of violence if it is constant. And those who marvel and exclaim and make such a fuss to find out the causes of this frailty in them, as if it were unnatural and not to be believed — how is it that they do not notice how often they are themselves guilty of the same, without any astonishment or miracle at all? It would perhaps be stranger to see the passion fixed; it is not a simply corporeal passion. If there is no end to avarice and ambition, there is doubtless no more to desire; it still lives after satiety; and it is impossible to prescribe either constant satisfaction or an end to it; it always goes beyond its possession. By this means inconstancy is perhaps in some sort more pardonable in them than in us; they may plead, as well as we do, the inclination to variety and novelty common to us both; and secondly, that, without us, they buy a cat in a sack. Joanna, queen of Naples, had her first husband, Andreas, hanged at the bars of her window in a halter of gold and silk woven with her own hand, because in matrimonial performance she found neither his parts nor his abilities answered the expectation she had conceived from his stature, beauty, youth, and activity, by which she had been caught and deceived. They may say that there is more work in doing than in suffering; and so, on their side they are always at least provided for necessity, whereas on ours it may fall out otherwise. For this reason Plato wisely made a law that, before marriage, to determine the fitness of the persons, the judges should see the young men who applied for it stripped naked, and the women only to the girdle. When they come to try us, perhaps they do not find us worthy of their choice:
"Experta latus, madidoque simillima loro Inguina, nec lassa stare coacta manu, Deserit imbelles thalamos."
["After every endeavour to arouse him to action, she quits the barren couch." — Martial, vii. 58.]
It is not enough that a man's will be good; weakness and insufficiency are lawful grounds for breaking a marriage,
"Et quaerendum aliunde foret nervosius illud, Quod posset zonam solvere virgineam:"
["And one must look elsewhere for a more vigorous lover, one who could undo her virgin girdle." — Catullus, lxvii. 27.]
why not? And, by her own measure, an amorous intelligence more licentious and active —
"Si blando nequeat superesse labori."
["If his strength be unequal to the pleasant task." — Virgil, Georg., iii. 127.]
But is it not great impudence to offer our imperfections and weaknesses where we want to please and leave a good opinion and esteem of ourselves? For the little I am able to do now:
"Ad unum Mollis opus."
["Fit but for once." — Horace, Epod., xii. 15.]
I would not trouble a woman I am to revere and fear:
"Fuge suspicari, Cujus undenum trepidavit aetas Claudere lustrum."
["Do not suspect a man whose eleventh lustrum is closed." — Horace, Od., ii. 4, 12 — actually it limits this to the eighth.]

Nature should be satisfied to have made this age miserable, without also making it ridiculous. I hate to see it, for one poor inch of pitiful vigour that visits but thrice a week, strut and put itself forward with as much eagerness as if it were about to perform mighty feats — a true flax-flame; and laugh to see it so boil and bubble, and then in a moment so frozen and out. This appetite ought to belong only to the flower of beautiful youth: don't trust it to second that indefatigable, full, constant, magnanimous ardour you think is in you, for it will certainly leave you in a pretty corner; but rather transfer it to some tender, bashful, ignorant boy, who still trembles at the rod and blushes:
"Indum sanguineo veluti violaverit ostro Si quis ebur, vel mista rubent ubi lilia multa Alba rosa."
["As Indian ivory streaked with crimson, or white lilies mixed with the damask rose." — Aeneid, xii. 67.]
Whoever can wait till morning without dying of shame to see the disdain in the fair eyes of her who knows so well his fumbling incompetence,
"Et taciti fecere tamen convicia vultus,"
["Though she says nothing, her looks betray her anger." — Ovid, Amor., i. 7, 21.]

has never had the satisfaction and glory of having cudgelled them till they were weary, by the vigorous performance of one heroic night. When I have seen any one vexed with me, I have not at once accused her fickleness; I have been in doubt whether I did not have more reason to complain of nature; she has doubtless treated me very uncivilly and unkindly:
"Si non longa satis, si non bene mentula crassa Nimirum sapiunt, videntque parvam Matronae quoque mentulam illibenter:"

[The first verse is from an epigram in the Veterum Poetarum Catalecta, and the two others from an epigram in the same collection (Ad Matronas). They state Montaigne's charge against nature in terms not easily translated, indicated in the passage above.]
and done me a most enormous injury. Every limb I have, as much as any other, is equally my own, and none other more properly makes me a man than this.

I owe my whole picture to the public. The wisdom of my instruction lies in liberty, in truth, in essence: scorning to introduce those little, made-up, common, and provincial rules into the catalogue of its real duties — duties all natural, general, and constant, of which civility and ceremony are daughters indeed, but illegitimate. We are sure to have the vices of appearance, once we have had those of essence; once we have done with these, we run full tilt at the others, if it must be so; for there is danger that we shall invent new offices to excuse our negligence toward the natural ones, and to confound them. To show this — is it not seen that in places where faults are crimes, crimes are only faults; that in nations where the laws of decency are most rare and most lax, the primitive laws of common reason are best observed? The countless multitude of so many duties stifles and dissipates our care. The application of ourselves to light and trivial things diverts us from those that are necessary and just. Oh, how easily and plausibly these superficial men take their way, compared to ours! These are shadows with which we paper one another over; but we do not pay; we only inflame the reckoning to be made with that great judge who tucks up our rags and tatters above our shameful parts, and does not flinch from viewing us all over, even to our inmost and most secret filth. It would be a useful decency of our maidenly modesty if it could keep him from this discovery. In short, whoever could reclaim man from such a scrupulous verbal superstition would do the world no great disservice. Our life is divided between folly and prudence; whoever writes about it only what is reverend and canonical will leave more than half of it behind. I do not excuse myself to myself; and if I did, it would be rather for my excuses I would excuse myself than for any other fault. I excuse myself of certain humours, which I think stronger in number than those on my side. With that consideration, I will say further (since I wish to please everyone, hard as that will be):
"Esse unum hominem accommodatum ad tantam morum ac sermonum et voluntatum varietatem,"
["That one man should accommodate himself to such a variety of manners, discourses, and wills." — Q. Cicero, De Pet. Consul, c. 14.]

that they ought not to condemn me for putting forward, as authorities, things received and approved by so many ages; and that there is no reason that for want of rhyme they should refuse me the liberty they grant even to churchmen of our nation and time — and these among the most notable. Here are two of their lively verses:
"Rimula, dispeream, ni monogramma tua est."
"Un vit d'amy la contente et bien traicte:"
[St Gelais, Œuvres Poétiques, p. 99, ed. Lyons, 1574.]

and how many others. I love modesty; and it is not out of judgment that I have chosen this scandalous way of speaking; nature has chosen it for me. I don't commend it, any more than other forms that go against common use; but I excuse it, and by both general and particular circumstances soften the accusation against it.
But to go on. Where, too, can it come from, that usurpation of sovereign authority you take to yourself over the women, who favour you at their own expense,
"Si furtiva dedit mira munuscula nocte,"
["If, in the stealthy night, she has made strange little gifts." — Catullus, lxviii. 145.]

such that you presently take up the interest, coolness, and authority of a husband? It is a free contract — why do you not then keep to it, as you would have them do? There is no prescription on voluntary matters. It is against the form, but it is true that in my time I have conducted this bargain, as much as the nature of it would permit, as conscientiously and with as much colour of justice as any other contract; and that I never pretended any other affection than what I really had, and have truthfully acquainted them with its birth, vigour, and decline, its fits and lulls. A man does not always hold on at the same rate. I have been so sparing of my promises that I think I have done better than my word. They have found me faithful even to the service of their inconstancy, a confessed and sometimes repeated inconstancy. I never broke with them while I had any hold at all; and whatever cause they have given me, never broke with them to hatred or contempt; for such intimacies, however scandalously obtained, do oblige one to some goodwill. I have sometimes shown, at their tricks and evasions, a little indiscreet anger and impatience; for I am naturally subject to rash emotions, which, light and short as they are, often spoil my market. When they have consulted my judgment, I have never stuck at giving them sharp paternal counsels, and pinching them to the quick. If I have left them any cause to complain of me, it is rather of finding in me a love foolishly conscientious by comparison with modern usage than anything else. I have kept my word in things from which I might easily have been dispensed; they have sometimes surrendered themselves with reputation, and on terms that they would have been willing enough should be broken by the conqueror. I have, more than once, made pleasure, at its greatest height, give way to the interest of their honour; and where reason urged me, have armed them against myself, so that they conducted themselves more decorously and securely by my rules, when they frankly referred themselves to them, than they would have done by their own. I have ever, as much as I could, taken on myself alone the hazard of our assignations, to clear them; and have always contrived our meetings after the hardest and most unusual manner, as less suspected and, in my opinion, more accessible. They are most open where they think themselves most securely shut up; things least feared are least forbidden and observed. One may more boldly venture what nobody thinks you would venture, which by its difficulty becomes easy. Never did any man make his approaches more impertinently obvious; this way of loving is more according to discipline, but how ridiculous it is to our people, and how ineffective, no one knows better than I; yet I shall not repent of it; I have nothing more there to lose:
"Me tabula sacer Votiva paries, indicat uvida Suspendisse potenti Vestimenta maris deo:"
["The holy wall, by my votive tablet, shows that I have hung up my wet clothes in honour of the mighty god of the sea." — Horace, Od., i. 5, 13.]
it is now time to speak out. But as I might perhaps say to another, "You are talking idly, my friend; the love of your time has little dealing with faith and integrity":
"Haec si tu postules Ratione certa facere, nihilo plus agas, Quam si des operam, ut cum ratione insanias:"
["If you seek to make these things certain by reason, you will get no further than if you tried to be sanely mad." — Terence, Eun., act i., sc. 1, v. 16.]

on the contrary, also, if it were for me to begin over again, it would certainly be by the same method and the same progress, however fruitless it might be for me; folly and inability are commendable in an uncommendable action. The further I go from their humour in this, the closer I come to my own. As for the rest, in this traffic I did not let myself be wholly carried away; I pleased myself in it, but did not forget myself. I kept entire, for their service and my own, the little sense and discretion nature has given me: a little emotion, but no dotage. My conscience too was engaged in it, even to debauch and licentiousness; but as to ingratitude, treachery, malice, and cruelty, never. I would not purchase the pleasure of this vice at any price, but content myself with its proper and simple cost:
"Nullum intra se vitium est."
["Nothing is a vice in itself." — Seneca, Ep., 95.]

I almost equally hate a stupid sluggish laziness and a toilsome painful employment; the one pinches, the other puts me to sleep. I like wounds as well as bruises, and cuts as well as dull blows. I found in this commerce, when I was most able for it, a just moderation between these extremes. Love is a sprightly, lively, gay agitation; I was neither troubled nor afflicted with it, but heated, and indeed disordered; a man must stop there; it hurts nobody but fools. A young man asked the philosopher Panaetius if it was becoming for a wise man to be in love. "Let the wise man look to that," he answered, "but as for you and me, who are not so, let us not engage in so stirring and violent an affair, which enslaves us to others and makes us contemptible to ourselves." He spoke true: we are not to trust a thing so precipitous in itself to a soul that has not the wherewithal to withstand its assaults and to disprove in practice the saying of Agesilaus, that prudence and love cannot live together.
