It is a vain employment, true, unbecoming, shameful, and illegitimate; but carried on in this manner, I look on it as wholesome, fit to enliven a drowsy soul and to rouse a heavy body; and, as an experienced physician, I would prescribe it for a man of my form and condition, as soon as any other recipe, to rouse him and keep him in vigour till well advanced in years, and to put off the approaches of age. While we are still in the suburbs, and while the pulse still beats:
"Dum nova canities, dum prima et recta senectus, Dum superest lachesi quod torqueat, et pedibus me Porto meis, nullo dextram subeunte bacillo,"

["While my white hair is new, while old age is still upright-shouldered, while there is still something for Lachesis to spin, while I can walk on my own legs and need no staff to lean upon." — Juvenal, iii. 26.]

we have need to be prodded and tickled by some such sharp incentive as this. Just see what youth, vigour, and gaiety it inspired in good Anacreon; and Socrates, then older than I am, speaking of an amorous object:

"Leaning," said he, "my shoulder to her shoulder and my head to hers, as we were reading together in a book, I felt, without dissembling, a sudden sting in my shoulder like the biting of an insect, which I still felt above five days afterwards; and a continual itching crept into my heart." So a merely accidental touch, and that of a shoulder, heated and altered a soul cooled and enervated by age, and the strictest liver of all mankind. And, indeed, why not? Socrates was a man, and would not be, nor seem, anything else. Philosophy does not contend against natural pleasures, provided they are moderate, and only preaches moderation, not total abstinence; the power of its resistance is exerted against those that are adulterate and strange. Philosophy says that the appetites of the body ought not to be heightened by the mind, and ingeniously warns us not to stir up hunger by being already full; not to stuff, instead of merely filling, the belly; to avoid all enjoyments that may bring us to want, and all meats and drinks that bring thirst and hunger; just as in the service of love, philosophy prescribes that we take such an object as may simply satisfy the body's need, and does not stir the soul, which ought only barely to follow and assist the body without mixing in the affair. But have I not reason to hold that these precepts, which in my opinion are somewhat over-strict, only concern a body in its best plight, and that in a body broken by age, as in a weak stomach, it is excusable to warm and support it by art, and by the mediation of fancy to restore the appetite and cheerfulness it has lost of itself?

May we not say that there is nothing in us, during this earthly imprisonment, that is purely either corporeal or spiritual; and that we injuriously break up a man alive; and that it seems only reasonable we should carry ourselves at least as favourably toward the use of pleasure as we do toward that of pain? Pain was, for example, vehement, even to perfection, in the souls of the saints by penitence; the body there naturally had a share, by right of union, and yet could have had little part in the cause; and yet they were not content for the body merely to follow and assist the afflicted soul: they have afflicted it with grievous and special torments, so that by the emulation of one another, the soul and body might plunge man into a misery the more salutary the more severe. In the same way, is it not injustice, in bodily pleasures, to subdue and keep down the soul, and say that it must therein be dragged along as to some forced, servile obligation and necessity? Rather, it is the soul's part to hatch and cherish them, there to present herself and to invite them — the authority of ruling belonging to her; just as it is also her part, in my opinion, in the pleasures proper to her, to inspire and infuse into the body all the feeling it is capable of, and to study how to make them sweet and useful to it. For it is good reason, as they say, that the body should not pursue its appetites to the prejudice of the mind; but why is it not also reasonable that the mind should not pursue hers to the prejudice of the body?

I have no other passion to keep me in breath. What avarice, ambition, quarrels, lawsuits do for others who, like me, have no particular vocation, love would do for me much more conveniently; it would give me back vigilance, sobriety, grace, and the care of my person; it would steady my countenance, so that the grimaces of old age — those deformed and dismal looks — would not come to disgrace it; it would put me again on sound and wise studies, by which I might make myself more loved and esteemed, clearing my mind of the despair of itself and of its use, and reintroducing it to itself; it would divert me from a thousand troublesome thoughts and melancholy humours that idleness and the ill posture of our health load us with at this age; it would warm again, at least in dreams, the blood that nature is abandoning; it would hold up the chin, and a little stretch the nerves, the vigour and cheerfulness of that poor man who is going full drive toward his ruin. But I very well understand that it is a thing hard to recover; by weakness and long experience, our taste has become more delicate and nice; we ask the most when we bring the least, and are hardest to choose when we least deserve to be accepted; and knowing ourselves for what we are, we are less confident and more distrustful. Nothing can assure us of being loved, considering our condition and theirs. I am ashamed to see myself in the company of those young wanton creatures:
"Cujus in indomito constantior inguine nervus, Quam nova collibus arbor inhaeret."
["In whose unbridled loins the vigour holds firmer than the young tree on the hills." — Horace, Epod., xii. 19.]
Why should we go and insinuate our misery into their gay and sprightly humour?
"Possint ut juvenes visere fervidi. Multo non sine risu, Dilapsam in cineres facem."
["That ardent youths may see, not without much laughter, a burning torch worn to ashes." — Horace, Od., iv. 13, 21.]

They have strength and reason on their side; let us give way; we have no business there. And these blossoms of springing beauty will not let themselves be handled by such numbed hands or dealt with by mere material means; for as the old philosopher answered one who jeered him because he could not gain the favour of a young girl he was making love to: "Friend, the hook won't stick in such soft cheese." It is a commerce that requires reciprocity and correspondence; the other pleasures we receive can be acknowledged by recompenses of another nature, but this one is not to be paid except in the same coin. In earnest, in this sport, the pleasure I give tickles my imagination more than what they give me does; now, the man has nothing of generosity in him who can receive pleasure where he confers none — it must be a mean soul that owes everything, and is content to maintain relations with people to whom he is a continual burden. There is no beauty, grace, or privacy so exquisite that a gentleman ought to want it at that rate. If they can only be kind to us out of pity, I had much rather die than live on charity. I would have the right to ask, in the style I heard them beg in Italy, "Fate ben per voi," or after the manner Cyrus exhorted his soldiers, "Whoever loves himself, let him follow me." "Consort yourself," someone will say, "with women of your own condition, whom a like fortune will make easier to your desire." Oh, ridiculous and insipid composition!
"Nolo Barbam vellere mortuo leoni."
["I will not pluck the beard from a dead lion." — Martial.]

Xenophon lays it as an objection and accusation against Menon, that he never made love to any but old women. For my part, I take more pleasure in just seeing the just and sweet mingling of two young beauties, or only thinking of it in my fancy, than in being myself an actor in some pitiful and imperfect conjunction;
[Which Cotton renders, "Than to be myself an actor in the second with a deformed creature."]
I leave that fantastic appetite to the Emperor Galba, who was only for old curried flesh; and to this poor wretch:
"O ego Di faciant talem to cernere possim, Caraque mutatis oscula ferre comis, Amplectique meis corpus non pingue lacertis!"
[Ovid, who (Ex Ponto, i. 4, 49) writes to his wife, "O may the gods grant that I might see you so, and bring dear kisses to your changed locks, and embrace your withered body in my arms."]

Among chief deformities I count forced and artificial beauties. Hemon, a young boy of Chios, thinking by fine dressing to get the beauty that nature had denied him, came to the philosopher Arcesilaus and asked him if it were possible for a wise man to be in love. "Yes," he replied, "provided it be not with a painted and adulterated beauty like yours."
[Diogenes Laertius, iv. 36. The question was whether a wise man could love him. Cotton has "Emonez, a young courtesan of Chios."]

Ugliness of a confessed antiquity is to me less old and less ugly than another that is polished and plastered up. Shall I say it, at the risk of having my throat cut? Love, in my opinion, is not properly and naturally in its season except in the age next to childhood,
"Quem si puellarum insereres choro, Mille sagaces falleret hospites, Discrimen obscurum, solutis Crinibus ambiguoque vultu:"
["Whom if you should place in a company of girls, a thousand sharp-eyed strangers would fail to tell him from them, with his loose locks and ambiguous look." — Horace, Od., ii. 5, 21.]

nor beauty either; for whereas Homer extends it as far as the budding of the beard, Plato himself has noted this as rare. The reason why the sophist Bion so pleasantly called the first appearing hairs of adolescence "Aristogitons" and "Harmodiuses" is well known. In virility I find it already somewhat out of date, though not as much as in old age;
"Importunus enim transvolat aridas Quercus."
["For it rudely passes over withered oaks." — Horace, Od., iv. 13, 9.]

and Marguerite, queen of Navarre, like a woman, very generously extends the advantage of women, ordaining that it is time at thirty to convert the title "fair" into "good." The shorter the authority we give to love over our lives, the better for us. Just look at his bearing — he is a beardless boy. Who does not know how, in his school, things proceed contrary to all order? Study, exercise, and usage are their ways to insufficiency; there novices rule:
"Amor ordinem nescit."
["Love knows no rule." — St Jerome, Letter to Chromatius.]

Without question his conduct is much more graceful when mixed with inadvertency and trouble; missteps and ill successes give him point and grace. Provided it is sharp and eager, it doesn't much matter whether it is prudent or not. Just see how he goes reeling, tripping, and playing; you put him in the stocks when you guide him by art and wisdom; and he is robbed of his divine liberty when put into those hairy, callous clutches.

As to the rest, I often hear the women set out this exchange as entirely spiritual, and disdain to consider the part the senses play in it; everything there serves; but I can say that I have often seen us excuse weaknesses in their understanding in favour of their outward beauty, but never yet seen that, in favour of mind, however mature and full, any of them would hold out a hand to a body even slightly in decline. Why does some one of them not take it into her head to make that noble Socratic bargain between body and soul, purchasing a philosophical and spiritual intelligence, and generation, at the price of her thighs, which is the highest price she can get for them? Plato ordains in his Laws that he who has done any signal and advantageous exploit in war may not be refused, throughout the campaign, his age or ugliness notwithstanding, a kiss or any other amorous favour from any woman whatever. What he thinks so just in honour of military valour — why may it not be the same in honour of any other good quality? And why does not some woman take a fancy to gain over her companions the glory of this chaste love? I may well say chaste:
"Nam si quando ad praelia ventum est, Ut quondam in stipulis magnus sine viribus ignis, Incassum furit:"
["For when they sometimes engage in love's battle, his sterile ardour blazes up only as a fire of straw." — Virgil, Georg., iii. 98.]
the vices that are stifled in the thought are not the worst.
To conclude this notable commentary, which has escaped me in a torrent of babble, a torrent sometimes impetuous and harmful,

"Ut missum sponsi furtivo munere malum Procurrit casto virginis a gremio, Quod miserae oblitae molli sub veste locatuat, Dum adventu matris prosilit, excutitur, Atque illud prono praeceps agitur decursu Huic manat tristi conscius ore rubor."

["As when an apple, sent by a lover as a secret gift to his mistress, falls from the chaste virgin's bosom, where she had quite forgotten it; when, starting at her mother's coming in, it is shaken out and rolls headlong over the floor before her eyes, a conscious blush covers her face." — Catullus, lxv. 19.]

I say that males and females are cast in the same mould, and that, education and habit excepted, the difference is not great. Plato indifferently invites both the one and the other to the society of all studies, exercises, and vocations, military and civil, in his Commonwealth; and the philosopher Antisthenes rejected any distinction between their virtue and ours. It is much easier to accuse one sex than to excuse the other; as the saying goes,
"Le fourgon se moque de la paele." ["The Pot and the Kettle."]
